sens: Son of Joktan
Descendant of a pre-flood patriarchal lineage
Eponymous ancestor of a region or people
H2700.detail:
1. Hatsarmaveth is a man who lived during the time of the patriarchs, son of Joktan and brother of twelve other sons including Sheba and Ophir. He appears in the genealogy of the descendants of Shem in Genesis 10:26 and 1 Chronicles 1:20.
2. His name literally means "village of death." Like many names in this genealogy, it likely evokes a geographical location or a people that bore his name among the ancient peoples of Arabia.
3. In biblical tradition, the sons of Joktan are presented as the ancestors of the peoples and regions of southern Arabia, with Hatsarmaveth presumably linked to a region or group from that area.
H2700.origine: The name Hatsarmaveth combines the Hebrew "hatzar" (village, encampment) and "maveth" (death). It is a typical geographical name from the table of nations in Genesis 10, where each son of Joktan apparently represents a city, region, or people of ancient Arabia. The same genealogy is repeated in 1 Chronicles 1, showing the importance of this list in biblical tradition.
H2700.emploi: Hatsarmaveth appears only twice in the Bible, both times in genealogical lists: in Genesis 10:26 as the third son of Joktan, and in 1 Chronicles 1:20 in the same enumeration. These two passages are parallel and are part of the table of nations that lists the descendants of Noah after the flood. He plays no active role in the biblical narrative; he is mentioned only as a link in the genealogical chain connecting ancient peoples to the patriarchs.

sens: City in southern Judah assigned to the tribe of Simeon
H2701.detail: Hatsar-Susa is a small city in the extreme southern part of Judah, in the desert region of the Negev. It was assigned to the tribe of Simeon during the division of the Promised Land (Joshua 19:5). Its name literally means "enclosure of horses" or "village of horses," suggesting that it was a place where horses were kept — likely royal horses intended for the army of the king of Israel.
H2701.origine: The name Hatsar-Susa combines two Hebrew words: hatsar ("enclosure," "courtyard") and susa ("horses"). This composition shows that the place was known for the function it served: a depot or pasture for horses. Such sites were important in the royal administration of Israel, especially under the reign of Solomon, who had considerable military needs for mounts.
H2701.emploi: Hatsar-Susa appears only once in the Bible, in Joshua 19:5, among the cities assigned to Simeon. It is listed among the localities of the southern Negev, an arid and sparsely populated region. Its extreme southern location indicates that it marked the boundary of Simeon's territory, in a difficult-to-access area. Although tradition associates this site with a place for storing royal horses, the biblical text does not provide additional details about its history or significance.
H2701.portee: This city reminds us that even minor, often forgotten localities had a place in God's plan for His people. Hatsar-Susa also testifies to the administrative wisdom of the kings of Israel, who organized the territory to support their army and defense. Its name invites us to reflect on divine providence in the concrete details of the life of the chosen people.

sens: Village of Simeon in ancient Canaan
H2702.detail: Hatsar-Susim is a village located in the territory of the tribe of Simeon, in Canaan. The name literally means "village of horses" in Hebrew (hatsar = village, susim = horses), suggesting that this place may have been known for horse breeding. It appears in the list of cities owned by Simeon until the reign of David (1 Chronicles 4:31).
H2702.origine: The Hebrew name חֲצַר סוּסִים consists of two elements: חֲצַר (hatsar, "village" or "enclosure") and סוּסִים (susim, "horses"). This nominal composition was common for naming places according to their main characteristic. The name likely reflects the importance of horses in the economy or activity of this village.
H2702.emploi: Hatsar-Susim appears only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 4:31, in an enumeration of the cities of Simeon. This passage lists several villages that this tribe owned until the reign of David, a time when tribal boundaries and city organization likely changed. The context shows that it was an ancient territorial possession of Simeon.

sens: Fortified city at the northeastern border of Canaan
H2703.detail: Hatsar-Énon is a locality located at the northeastern edge of the Promised Land. Its name, composed of two Hebrew words, literally means "village of springs" or "enclosure of fountains," suggesting a place where waters spring forth. In the prophetic vision of Ezekiel, it marks a major geographical landmark: it is mentioned as a reference point for tracing the northern boundary of Canaan, in the line of borders that the prophet sees for the restored territory of Israel.
H2703.origine: The name comes from two Hebrew elements: "hatsar" (חֲצַר), which denotes an enclosure, a village, or a fortified courtyard, and "énon" (עֵינָן), which relates to eyes or springs. The image is of a place where water springs forth, a source of life in the desert. Other villages bear the same first element, such as Hatsar-Gaddah or Hatsar-Shual, all fortified or organized places in biblical geography.
H2703.emploi: Hatsar-Énon appears only once in the Bible, in Ezekiel 47:17, in the context of the prophet Ezekiel's vision regarding the borders of the restored territory of Israel. It is cited as a landmark for the northern boundary, between Damascus and the region of Hamath. It serves as a topographical reference to define the contours of the promised land in the future envisioned by the prophet.

sens: Fortified city in northeastern Canaan, marking the northern boundary of the territory of Israel
Strategic location on the border between Canaan and the northern regions
H2704.detail:
1. Hatsar-Énan is a village-fortress in northeastern Canaan, whose name means "village of fountains" in Hebrew. It is the pinnacle of the northern delimitation of the territory that God assigns to Israel after the conquest: the boundary "will reach Hatsar-Énan" (Numbers 34:9). It is also the starting point of the eastern boundary of the land (Numbers 34:10).
2. This locality also appears in the prophetic vision of Ezekiel regarding the future division of the territory among the tribes. Ezekiel 48:1 mentions it as a landmark of the northern boundary, near Damascus and Hamath, highlighting its strategic and geographical importance.
H2704.origine: The Hebrew name חֲצַר עֵינוֹן (Hatsar-Énan) consists of חֲצַר *hatsar* ("village" or "enclosure") and עֵינוֹן *énan* (related to fountains or springs of water). It is a site whose abundance of water gives it strategic value, typical of well-fortified border locations.
H2704.emploi: Hatsar-Énan appears three times in the Bible, all in contexts delineating the territory of Israel. In Numbers 34, it is used twice to trace the northern and eastern borders of the promised land: it is a key point in the description of the land boundaries that Israel is to occupy. Ezekiel 48 reiterates it in his vision of the future distribution of the territory among the twelve tribes, showing that it retains its role as a major geographical landmark even in eschatological promises. It is always linked to prestigious neighboring regions: Hamath, Damascus, the road to Hethlon.

sens: City in the south of Judah
Border locality of the tribe of Simeon
H2705.detail: Hatsar-Schual is a city located in the southern territory of Judah. The name literally means "village of the jackal" in Hebrew, reflecting an arid and sparsely populated landscape. It appears in the lists of cities assigned to Judah during the division of the Promised Land (Joshua 15:28) and is also mentioned as a residence of the Simeonites (1 Chronicles 4:28), suggesting that it was shared between the two tribes or that it changed hands over time. The city is regularly cited alongside Beer-Sheba, another important center in the Negev, indicating its role in the settlement network of southern Judea.
H2705.origine: The Hebrew name חֲצַר שׁוּעָל (Cha.tsar Shu.al) combines two words: חֲצַר (cha.tsar, "enclosure" or "village") and שׁוּעָל (shu.al, "jackal"). This composition of place names — a wild animal associated with a type of settlement — is common in the biblical geography of the Negev, reflecting the semi-desert lands where these creatures live.
H2705.emploi: Hatsar-Schual is mentioned four times in the Old Testament, always in geographical lists: in the distribution of cities between the tribes of Judah and Simeon (Joshua 15:28 and 19:3), in the residences of the Simeonites under David (1 Chronicles 4:28), and during the repopulation of Judea after the exile (Nehemiah 11:27). It invariably appears in the group of localities in the Negev, alongside Beer-Sheba and other towns in the region. No particular event is associated with it in the biblical narrative: it remains an administrative and residential city in the south.

sens: Rule, ordinance established by authority
Prescription, obligation imposed on someone
Limit, boundary, that which is predetermined
Covenant, pact established by God with His people
H2706G.detail:
1. The word designates an official rule, an ordinance promulgated by one who has authority. When Joseph "made it a law" in Egypt (Genesis 47:26), he established a rule that applies to all: one-fifth of the harvest goes to Pharaoh. It is a decree that creates a stable framework.

2. More generally, it refers to a particular obligation assigned to someone: a prescribed task, a rightful share, or a resolution that one imposes on oneself. The word emphasizes less the act of obeying than the thing itself that is fixed, ordered.

3. The word can also mark a limit or boundary: what is inscribed within the limits of what must be done. It conveys the idea of a moral or practical boundary that no one should cross.

4. In the relationship between God and Israel, "law" becomes the very heart of the covenant: the ordinances and statutes that God has established are the fabric of the pact. Observing His "laws" and "commandments" is to live within the covenant (Deuteronomy 26:17).
H2706G.origine: The Hebrew word choq comes from a root that means "to engrave, trace, inscribe." The image is that of a mark engraved, a prescription traced and unchangeable. This explains why the word carries both the idea of firmness and limitation: a law is something fixed, stable, that one does not cross. In the Greek Old Testament, this word often translates the laws and ordinances of Egypt or of God Himself.
H2706G.emploi: The word appears about 100 times in the Old Testament, primarily in Exodus, Leviticus, Deuteronomy, and in the Psalms, particularly Psalm 119 which celebrates its beauty. It first designates human decrees (Genesis 47:26, 1 Samuel 30:25), then the prescriptions and cultic practices of Moses (Exodus 12:24, Leviticus 6:11, 10:11). But its main usage is religious: it refers to the laws and ordinances of God in Deuteronomy (Deuteronomy 4:6-8, 6:1, 26:17), presented as just and wise, worthy of being observed and meditated upon. In the Psalms, especially 119, the word expresses the believer's tenderness for the divine law, his joy in observing it. The meaning nuances: sometimes external and prescriptive, sometimes internalized and loved.
H2706G.portee: Understanding that "law" in Hebrew is not primarily an anonymous constraint, but a fixed, grave, and just word that comes from a trustworthy authority. For Israel and the psalmist, observing the divine law was an expression of love towards God, not servitude. This sheds light on how the Gospel relates to the law: not by denying it, but by revealing that grace fulfills what the law promised.

sens: Decree, ordinance established by a sovereign authority
Portion, share or part assigned to someone under a rule
Prescribed task or duty fixed
Limit or term established in advance
Inalienable right, that which is due by custom or justice
H2706H.detail:
1. The word primarily designates a decree or ordinance promulgated by an authority — the king, the priest, or God Himself. It is a rule established with force, that imposes itself. Genesis 47:22 speaks of a "law of Pharaoh" in favor of the priests: it is a royal decree that guarantees their rights.

2. It also designates a portion or share allocated to someone according to a fixed rule. In Leviticus 7:34, the priests receive "by a perpetual law" the breast and shoulder of the sacrifices: this is not arbitrary, it is an established and permanent right.

3. The word applies to a prescribed task or assigned duty. It is what is fixed for someone to accomplish — an obligation that arises from their function or status.

4. It can also mean a limit or a defined term established in advance. In Job 14:13, the psalmist asks God to "set a term to which you will remember me": a predetermined temporal limit.

5. Finally, it expresses an inalienable right, something that is due to someone by right and justice. Leviticus 10:14 tells Aaron that the breast and shoulder are given to you "as your right": what belongs to you by a holy and unchangeable custom.
H2706H.origine: The Hebrew root evokes the idea of "to engrave" or "to inscribe" — as one engraves a law in stone or on a tablet. The word thus designates what is fixed, established, unchangeable. It belongs to the family of terms that express order, rule, and stability in the life of Israel. The choq is the law viewed as an imposed limit, as a framework that delineates what is permitted and what is due to each — in contrast to the "mitsvah" (commandment) which is more about the command obeyed out of love.
H2706H.emploi: The word appears 17 times in the Hebrew Bible, especially in the Pentateuch (Genesis, Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers) and in the Wisdom literature (Job, Proverbs). It is particularly frequent in the priestly laws: the portions due to the priests are "perpetual laws" (Leviticus 7:34, 24:9; Numbers 18:11). In Job and Proverbs, the word takes on a more personal hue: in Job 23:12, "the words of his mouth" are the choq of the wise man, his rule of life. In Ezekiel 16:27, it designates a tribute, a portion taken. The word thus expresses both civil or religious law and personal right or assigned duty.
H2706H.portee: Understanding this word helps to grasp how the Bible conceives of the Law not as arbitrary oppression, but as a just and merciful order: everyone receives their share, everyone knows their limits and rights. For the believer, it is a reminder that God establishes stable and equitable frameworks. It is also an invitation to recognize that the Law — even when demanding — is a blessing, a protection that delineates our freedom and guarantees communal order.

sens: Boundary or marked demarcation
Duration or moment fixed in advance
Rule or law imposed
Assigned portion or quantity
H2706I.detail:
1. A limit is primarily a boundary, a line that separates and delineates: God has "marked out a circle on the surface of the waters, as a limit between light and darkness" (Job 26:10), and He has given the sea "the sand for a limit, an eternal limit that it cannot cross" (Jeremiah 5:22). It is an established contour that imposes itself and cannot be exceeded.
2. A limit can also be a fixed term, a prescribed duration: "If his days are determined, if you have numbered his months, if you have set a limit that he cannot pass" (Job 14:5), speaks of the fateful moment when human life stops. It is the idea of an inevitable deadline.
3. A limit can be a prescription, a law that is imposed: God says, "When I imposed my law upon him, and set bars and doors" (Job 38:10), concerning the sea. It is the order established by authority.
4. A limit can designate a determined portion or measure: in the context of punishments (Isaiah 5:14), the "measure" speaks of a quantity that exceeds what was normal or fair.
H2706I.origine: The Hebrew word choq comes from a root meaning "to engrave, trace, write." The starting image is that of a mark engraved or a line drawn to delineate a space. From there comes the meaning of ordinance or decree: what is written, what is engraved in stone or in memory. The word has taken on a broad scope: everything that is prescribed, ordered, predetermined by an authority (especially God).
H2706I.emploi: The word choq appears 7 times in the provided usages, mainly in the Poetic books (Job and Proverbs) and the Prophets (Isaiah, Jeremiah). Its usage is dominated by the idea of a limit imposed by God on creation: on the waters (Job 26:10; Jeremiah 5:22; Proverbs 8:29), on the days of man (Job 14:5). It also designates a prescription or a "law" given by the Lord (Job 38:10). The word always carries a connotation of order, stability, and immutability: what is fixed does not change, what is limited does not cross its limit. That is why it is mainly found when speaking of the boundaries of the physical world and the limits of human life.
H2706I.portee: Understanding that God has established limits reassures and troubles us. It reassures, because the world is not chaos: the waters do not engulf the earth (Jeremiah 5:22), and death itself is a fixed term (Job 14:5). It troubles us, because this limit also concerns us: our days are numbered, our life is not infinite. The Christian sees in this the wisdom of God who "upholds the order of the world by His word": living according to the limits that God has set is to submit to His wisdom and find peace.

sens: To trace or carve lines into a surface (stone, wood, metal) to form a design or pattern
To paint or draw an image on a wall or flat surface
To mark deeply, leaving a lasting trace
H2707.detail: 1. The primary meaning is to trace lines by carving: to cut, dig, or incise a hard surface to form a pattern, design, or ornament. In the Temple of Jerusalem, King Solomon had cherubim, palms, and flowers engraved on the interior walls, then covered these engravings with gold (1 Kings 6:35); this is a work of a goldsmith or sculptor that gives relief and beauty to objects. 2. The word can also refer to the action of painting or drawing on a flat surface, without necessarily carving: images traced on the wall. In Jerusalem, the prophet Ezekiel discovered paintings of abominable animals and painted idols on the walls of the temple (Ezekiel 8:10), and other paintings of Chaldean men drawn in red (Ezekiel 23:14). 3. Figuratively, it means to leave a deep and lasting mark, like an inscription that cannot be erased; it is to imprint something indelibly.
H2707.origine: The Hebrew root חקה (chaqah) fundamentally means to cut, carve, or engrave. It is related to the idea of tracing a limit or a line by incision. The word evokes the image of a chisel that carves into the material, creating a visible and permanent form. This root belongs to the same family as חוק (choq), which means law or statute — because a law, like an engraving, traces a limit that cannot be crossed.
H2707.emploi: The word חָקָה appears four times in the Hebrew Bible, mainly in two contexts: first, the decorations of the Temple, where Solomon had religious motifs engraved (1 Kings 6:35); secondly, the denunciation of Israel's idolatries, where Ezekiel describes the paintings of idols and abominable figures painted in the Temple (Ezekiel 8:10 and 23:14). One occurrence is also found in Job 13:27. Translations vary between "sculpture," "painted," and "painting," as the Hebrew word covers both relief engravings and flat images drawn or painted. The emphasis is always on the visible, durable, and crafted trace.
H2707.portee: To engrave reminds us that our actions, words, and choices leave marks — some beautiful and glorious, like the ornaments of God's Temple, others dangerous and corrupt, like the painted idols that the Israelites worshiped. It is an invitation to examine what we "engrave" in our hearts and in the world: do we seek to honor God through our works, or do we allow the deceptive images of modern idols to imprint themselves in us? The Lord, on His part, engraves His name and His promises indelibly in the hearts of His children.

sens: Divine decree establishing what must be done or not done
Established rule intended to be permanent and constant
Custom or practice regularly observed
Limit or boundary that God has assigned to creation
H2708.detail: 1. A law in the strict sense: a commandment prescribed by God to His people, with authority and binding force. When Abraham "keeps the statutes of the Lord" (Genesis 26:5), he submits to rules that God has given him, as clearly seen in Leviticus where God enumerates His ritual and moral ordinances (Leviticus 18:4, 18:5). 2. A permanent ordinance: an institution established to last over time, a protocol that is repeated generation after generation. The Passover, for example, must be celebrated "as a perpetual law" (Exodus 12:14), and the priests must light the lamps of the sanctuary "according to a perpetual ordinance" (Exodus 27:21). 3. A customary or habitual practice: what nations do regularly according to their own traditions. Ezekiel reproaches Jerusalem for not following the ordinances of the Lord "as the nations do" (Ezekiel 5:7). 4. The limits that God has set on natural creation: Job speaks of the "statutes of heaven" (Job 38:33), the regular laws that govern the cosmic order, as Jeremiah reminds that the Lord "has established laws in heaven and on earth" (Jeremiah 31:35, 33:25).
H2708.origine: The Hebrew word chuqqah comes from a root meaning "to engrave" or "to trace" — the idea of inscribing something in a durable and unavoidable manner. A statute is what is engraved, decided once and for all. This word is very common in the Hebrew Bible, particularly in the books of the Law (Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers, Deuteronomy), where it designates the prescriptions of worship and moral life that Israel must observe.
H2708.emploi: The word appears about 100 times in the Hebrew Bible. It is a key term in legislative and cultic vocabulary. In Leviticus and Numbers, it often designates specific rites: the manner of celebrating the Passover (Exodus 12), the rules for offerings (Leviticus 3:17, 7:36), the fast of Yom Kippur (Leviticus 16:29, 16:31, 16:34). In Deuteronomy and the historical books, it expands to moral commandments and the covenant with God: keeping the laws is being faithful to the covenant (2 Kings 17:13; 2 Chronicles 7:19). The spiritual stakes increase: obeying the statutes of the Lord is to recognize Him as Lord; rejecting them is to break the covenant and attract a curse (Leviticus 26:15; Deuteronomy 28:15).
H2708.portee: For the Christian reader, this word reminds us that God is not arbitrary, but a wise legislator who establishes rules for our good. The biblical statutes reveal His holy and just character. Although the Christian is freed from the Mosaic Law by grace in Christ, this word invites us to recognize the authority and kindness of God: His ordinances always aim for our sanctification and true freedom.

sens: Head of a family among the exiles who returned from Babylon with Zerubbabel
H2709.detail: 1. Hakupha is a man who lived during the time of the Exile and the Return. His name appears in the lists of families of exiles who returned from Babylon with Zerubbabel, after the destruction of the temple in Jerusalem. He was the head of a family, and his descendants are listed among those who made the journey back to Jerusalem to rebuild the temple and the community.
H2709.origine: The Hebrew name חֲקוּפָא (Hakupha) means "bent" or "one who is folded," perhaps evoking a physical characteristic or an attitude. It is a family name among the ancient Levantine communities. The name appears identically in the two parallel lists of the return from exile, which shows the importance of this family in the reconstitution of the people after the Babylonian captivity.
H2709.emploi: Hakupha is mentioned only twice in the Bible, both times in the parallel lists of families returned from exile. In Ezra 2:51 and Nehemiah 7:53, he is listed among the heads of families of temple servants (the Nethinim), between the sons of Bakbuk and the sons of Harhur. These two passages report the same event — the return of the exiles from Babylon — with nearly identical nomenclature, indicating that Hakupha and his family played a role in the restoration of temple worship upon the return from exile.

sens: To mark, engrave, or inscribe something in stone, wood, or a surface
To draw lines, boundaries, or contours on a surface
To establish a law, decree a judgment or ordinance
To bear a scepter or staff of command
To establish or fix the boundaries and rules of the world
H2710.detail:
1. The most concrete meaning is to engrave or inscribe: to trace letters, signs, or images in stone or on a durable surface. Isaiah 49:16 provides a beautiful image: "Behold, I have engraved you on the palms of my hands." This marks something permanently.

2. From this derives the meaning of drawing lines or contours: Proverbs 8:27 speaks of one who "drew a circle on the face of the deep," meaning who delineated or marked the limits of creation.

3. The act of engraving a law takes on a legal sense: to decree, to establish an ordinance. Isaiah 10:1 denounces "those who pronounce iniquitous ordinances, and those who transcribe unjust decrees": to engrave a law is to establish it with authority.

4. The scepter or staff is the instrument of government: Genesis 49:10 says, "The scepter shall not depart from Judah," the scepter symbolizing royal power and the right to command.

5. Finally, when speaking of God who "traces" the boundaries of the world (Proverbs 8:29), the word evokes the establishment of immutable boundaries and rules that structure creation.
H2710.origine: The verb חָקַק comes from a root that expresses the idea of making marks, tracing. The basic image is physical: to engrave, to chisel into a hard material. This root also exists in Akkadian with a similar meaning. The noun חֹק (law, decree, ordinance) is a natural derivative: a law is something that has been marked, engraved, established durably. To engrave a law is to make it permanent and public, hence the transition from the concrete sense to the legal and political sense.
H2710.emploi: The verb appears 19 times in the Old Testament, mostly in the wisdom books (Proverbs, Job) and among the prophets. In Proverbs 8, divine Wisdom "traces" (drew) the limits of the world at creation. In political and legal contexts, the word designates one who establishes laws or governs: Isaiah 33:22 calls the Lord our "legislator," and Isaiah 10:1 speaks of those who "pronounce" iniquitous ordinances. In warrior passages (Judges 5, Psalms 60), the scepter and staff mark the power of the leader. The word can also mean to inscribe in a register (Job 19:23, where Job wishes that his words were written) or to trace a drawing (Ezekiel 4:1, where God commands to trace the city of Jerusalem). Its meaning thus varies from the concrete (to engrave, to trace) to the political (to decree, to govern).
H2710.portee: This word teaches that God's laws and decisions are not empty words, but realities engraved, established with authority and permanence. When it is said that God "traces" the boundaries of the world, it reminds us that all order, all framework, all justice comes from Him alone. For the believer, this invites meditation on the firmness of God's decrees and recognition of His sovereign authority over all human ordinances.

sens: Firm and determined decision
Rule, ordinance imposed
What is prescribed, fixed by an authority
H2711.detail:
1. A resolution is a decision made with firmness and determination. In Judges 5:15, it speaks of the "resolutions of the heart" of the princes of Issachar: it is the moral strength, the determination that drives them to act and follow Deborah and Barak into battle.
2. An ordinance is a rule established by an authority to be followed and obeyed. In Isaiah 10:1, the prophet condemns those who pronounce "iniquitous ordinances," that is, unjust rules that they impose by force on those who endure them.
3. More broadly, this word designates what is prescribed, fixed, established definitively: it is the action of an authority that decides and orders what must be done.
H2711.origine: This word is a variant of a more common Hebrew word (choq) meaning "decree" or "statute." It comes from a root that evokes the idea of tracing, engraving, marking something durably and irrevocably. The basic notion is that of a limit or a line drawn, hence the idea of rule and established order.
H2711.emploi: This Hebrew word appears only twice in the Bible in the French Segond. In Judges 5:15, in Deborah's song, it describes the firm and resolute thoughts of the heart. In Isaiah 10:1, it designates the decrees and unjust ordinances pronounced by the leaders of the people. In these two contexts, the word carries the idea of a determined will, whether it be intimate (resolution of the heart) or imposed by power (legal ordinance).
H2711.portee: This word reminds us that our resolutions — our deep decisions of the heart — are important in God's eyes. But it also warns us: human authority that pronounces unjust ordinances opposes divine justice. It invites us to have just resolutions and to refuse to follow iniquitous rules.

sens: City of the tribe of Naphtali
Border locality of Naphtali
H2712A.detail: Hukkok is a city located on the border of the territory of the tribe of Naphtali. It is mentioned as a landmark in the description of the boundaries of the land assigned to Naphtali after the conquest of Canaan (Joshua 19:34). This city marked a specific place where the territories of several tribes met: Naphtali, Zebulun, Asher, and Judah.
H2712A.origine: The name Hukkok means "established thing" or "fixed destiny," evoking a limit or an ordinance. It carries the sense of what is stopped, marked, defined — in this case, a territorial boundary established by God during the division of Canaan among the tribes of Israel.
H2712A.emploi: Hukkok appears only once in the Bible, in Joshua 19:34, during the account of the division of the lands among the tribes of Israel after the conquest of Canaan. It is listed among the border cities of Naphtali, serving to precisely delineate the territory of this tribe against its neighbors. The context shows that it was an important geographical landmark for marking the limits of the heritage assigned to each tribe.
H2712A.portee: Hukkok reminds us that God precisely ordered the division of Canaan among the tribes of Israel. This discreet mention of a small border city affirms that each tribe received a determined share of the Promised Land, according to a plan established by the Lord. It is a testimony to the fulfillment of the divine promises made to the patriarchs.

sens: City of the tribe of Asher
H2712B.detail: Hukok is a city that belonged to the tribe of Asher, one of the twelve tribes of Israel. It is mentioned in 1 Chronicles 6:75 as one of the cities assigned to the Levites, along with its surrounding lands. This city is also known by the alternative name Helkath.
H2712B.origine: The name Hukok comes from Hebrew and literally means "assigned" or "designated" — the idea of something that has been determined or established. It is a geographical name whose root evokes an allocation or a fixed destination, which fits well with a city officially assigned to the Levites for their habitation and pastures.
H2712B.emploi: Hukok is mentioned only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 6:75, in the list of Levitical cities. It was located in the territory of Asher, in northern Israel. This enumeration was part of the administrative organization established after the conquest, where certain fortified cities were reserved for the descendants of Levi, who did not receive their own territory but lived dispersed among the other tribes.

sens: to search, to look into detail
to explore a place or subject
to verify the truth or authenticity of something
to probe thoughts, intentions, or feelings
H2713.detail:
1. The word describes the action of searching or looking carefully. In Deuteronomy 13:14, the one investigating an accusation of idolatry must "examine" the facts carefully to verify if the abomination has truly occurred.
2. It can also mean to explore or systematically survey a place: in Judges 18:2, the scouts go to "reconnoiter" the land of Canaan to assess the terrain.
3. The word takes on a broader meaning: to verify accuracy or authenticity. In 1 Kings 7:47, Solomon does not "check" the exact weight of all his bronze utensils because they are too numerous.
4. Finally, it describes the divine action of scrutinizing the heart and the reins — the hidden thoughts and motivations. Jeremiah 17:10 states that the Lord "tests" the heart and "searches" the reins to judge according to each person's ways.
H2713.origine: The root חקר (cha.qar) evokes the image of digging, penetrating deeply to discover what is hidden or unknown. It belongs to an ancient Semitic family concerning investigation and research. The word often translates the idea of a meticulous inquiry or systematic exploration: the subject seeks to know what is not immediately visible or obvious.
H2713.emploi: The verb appears 26 times in the Old Testament, especially in the wisdom books (Job, Proverbs, Ecclesiastes) and the historical books. In legal or judicial texts (Deuteronomy, Samuel), it describes the official inquiry to establish the facts. In the Psalms and among the prophets (Jeremiah), it evokes the divine examination of human intentions: God "searches" hearts and reins, which emphasizes His omniscience. In Proverbs 23:30 or 25:2, the verb takes on nuances: tasting wine, or exploring a mystery. The major theological usage shows it applied to God alone, who scrutinizes hearts as no one else can.
H2713.portee: This word reminds the Christian that God does not merely observe the surface of things: He knows the hidden thoughts, the most secret intentions of the heart. It is both a call to inner honesty and a comfort: nothing escapes the One who knows us completely. For the believer, it is also a model of right discernment: to thoroughly examine words, motives, and facts before judging or acting.

sens: That which cannot be fathomed, measured, or understood by human reason
The action of seeking to understand or examine something
That which exceeds ordinary experience and knowledge
H2714.detail:
1. That which cannot be fathomed, measured, or understood by human reason: it refers to what escapes our ability to search and know. Psalm 145:3 applies it to the greatness of God: "His greatness is unsearchable," we cannot measure its limits. Similarly, Job 11:7 asks: "Do you claim to fathom the thoughts of God?" — it is impossible, they are too high, too deep.
2. The action of seeking to understand or examine something closely: the word denotes the work of one who digs, who asks questions to know. In Job 8:8, it is recommended to "search" the experience of the ancients, that is, to question them to learn what they have discovered. It is an active effort of inquiry and reflection.
3. That which exceeds ordinary experience and knowledge: in Judges 5:16, the "deliberations" of the heart of Reuben are intimate, secret thoughts that cannot be seen from the outside. Job 36:26 says of the Almighty that "the number of His years is unsearchable" — it is beyond what can be counted or known.
H2714.origine: The word comes from a root meaning "to examine, to dig, to search." In Hebrew, it is close to the verb that expresses the action of scrutinizing, searching deeply. The image is that of an active search, an inquiry conducted to discover the truth. When something is unsearchable, it means that all the digging and effort in the world cannot penetrate it.
H2714.emploi: This word appears 12 times in the Old Testament, especially in Job and the Psalms. It is often used to say that God's wisdom, power, and thoughts are unsearchable — we cannot reach or fully understand them (Job 5:9, Job 9:10, Job 36:26, Psalms 145:3, Isaiah 40:28). Elsewhere, it designates the human action of seeking or examining: searching the experience of the ancients (Job 8:8), examining one's own heart (Judges 5:16), or undertaking research (Proverbs 25:27). The meaning changes according to the context: when it is God or His mysteries, it is the unsearchable; when it is man acting, it is the search, the inquiry.
H2714.portee: This word reminds the reader that God infinitely surpasses our understanding. This is not a frustration: it is an invitation to humility and trust. We cannot confine God within our categories, and this is a reason to worship Him rather than pretend to master Him. At the same time, it encourages us to seek and question — to "search" the experience of the wise — without believing that we will ever reach absolute understanding.

sens: Man of high rank, member of the social elite
Person invested with official authority, magistrate or administrator
Person of free and illustrious birth, as opposed to a slave
H2715.detail:
1. The word primarily designates a man who occupies a high position in society, respected by his peers. In 1 Kings 21:8, Jezebel writes to the "great ones" of the city of Naboth to involve them in a plot: these men are clearly influential notables.
2. It also specifically applies to magistrates and officials who exercise authority. In Nehemiah 2:16, Nehemiah speaks of the "magistrates" who were unaware of his comings and goings, showing that this term refers to those who manage public affairs.
3. Finally, it refers to the condition of freedom and dignity. A "great one" is born free, of good lineage, in contrast to one who depends on a master. This dimension appears in the implicit contrast: it is the noble-born man who can hold a position of responsibility.
H2715.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root expressing the idea of "freedom" or "free birth." In the Old Testament, it stands in opposition to slavery: a great one is a man born freely, who enjoys rights and status. The notion has evolved over time: from simple freedom, it has come to encompass social dignity, and then administrative power. This is why the Segond translates the same word sometimes as "great" and sometimes as "magistrate": the context clarifies whether the emphasis is on social rank or official function.
H2715.emploi: This word appears 13 times in the Old Testament, concentrated mainly in Nehemiah (where Nehemiah interacts with the great ones and magistrates who help him rebuild Jerusalem) and in a few passages from Isaiah and Jeremiah. In Nehemiah 4:19, the "great ones" are the leaders of the people to whom Nehemiah addresses himself to encourage them in the reconstruction. In Isaiah 34:12, it is a cry of ruin: "There will be no more great ones to proclaim a king" — the word then refers to the dignitaries of a state. The meaning always oscillates between high social status and official charge, but in all cases, it refers to men who matter and who make decisions.
H2715.portee: This word reminds us that the Bible views social hierarchies and public responsibilities without denial. It does not condemn the existence of the "great ones" — it calls them to act with justice. Nehemiah rebukes the great ones of Judah when they profane the Sabbath (13:17): the height of rank does not exempt one from obeying God. It is a call to the conscience of the responsible.

sens: Become dry, lose moisture
Cease to flow, referring to a water source
Completely dry up, become desiccated
Be drained, be emptied of water
H2717A.detail:
1. The primary meaning is very concrete: to become dry, to lose moisture. After the Flood, the waters recede and "the surface of the earth had dried" (Genesis 8:13) — it is a simple drying, like a rope that dries after washing (Judges 16:8).
2. The word then designates the drying up of watercourses: they "dry up," meaning they cease to flow and eventually disappear. Job expresses it this way: "The rivers dry up and become desiccated" (Job 14:11), an image of death that dries up all life.
3. It can also express complete and lasting desiccation. "The waters of the sea will dry up, the river will become dry and arid" (Isaiah 19:5): this is a calamity, a divine judgment that transforms living water into a barren desert.
4. When speaking of God, the verb takes on a dimension of power: God "dried up the sea" (Isaiah 51:10), He "will dry up all the rivers" (Isaiah 37:25). It is an act of sovereign domination over nature.
H2717A.origine: The Hebrew root חרב (ḥarēb) first evokes the state of being dry, emptied of water. It is linked to the image of desiccation: what loses its moisture dies. The noun חרב can also mean "ruin" or "desolation," as a dry land is a devastated land. The family of the word includes terms that all express this deprivation of water and the death it entails.
H2717A.emploi: This verb appears 15 times in the Hebrew Bible, mainly among the prophets (Isaiah, Jeremiah, Hosea, Nahum). It first describes natural realities: after the Flood, the earth dries (Genesis 8:13); the ropes dry (Judges 16:8). But it becomes primarily a language of divine judgment: the prophets announce that God will dry up the waters as a sign of condemnation (Isaiah 19:5-6, Jeremiah 51:36). It also evokes God's power at the time of the Exodus: God dried up the Red Sea to save His people (Isaiah 51:10). The verb can be active (someone dries up) or passive (something becomes dry).
H2717A.portee: This word helps the reader understand how the Bible speaks of divine judgment and the power of God. The drying up of waters is both a calamity (the end of life) and a sign of the sovereign intervention of the Lord. That is why it often appears in oracles against the nations: drying up rivers means destroying wealth and power. But it is also what God did at the Flood and at the Red Sea to save His people. The word reminds us that God has mastery even over the elements of nature.

sens: Completely destroy, annihilate
Reduce to ruins, demolish
Render desolate, leave empty and lifeless
Be reduced to a state of ruin or desolation
H2717B.detail:
1. The verb חָרֵב first evokes the violent action of destroying: to destroy a country, a city, a sanctuary (Ezekiel 6:6: "your cities will be ruined"). It is to ravage with force, to annihilate, to tear apart — the image of total and deliberate destruction.
2. The word also designates the result of this destruction: the ruins that remain, the state of desolation of a place (Ezekiel 26:2: Tyre says of Jerusalem, "it is desolate"). A ruined city is empty, abandoned, dead.
3. In particular, the verb expresses the annihilation of places of worship and altars: when God "ravages" the high places of idols (Ezekiel 6:6), He destroys their religious power. It is a divine judgment that renders sterile and unusable what served for evil.
4. Finally, חָרֵב can describe the passive state of being ruined, devastated, reduced to nothing (Isaiah 37:18: "the kings of Assyria have ravaged all the countries"). The subject undergoes destruction, it is emptied, stripped of its essence.
H2717B.origine: The verb חָרֵב comes from a Hebrew root that evokes the idea of burning, drying, reducing to nothing. The underlying image is that of a land dried up, a world desertified by fire or violence. The family of the word includes forms that intensify this notion: one can "ravage" (action) or be "ravaged" (result). In Aramaic, the parallel form חֲרַב (charav) carries the same meaning of desolation and destruction.
H2717B.emploi: The verb חָרֵב appears 18 times in the Old Testament, concentrated mainly in the prophets (Isaiah, Ezekiel, Jeremiah) and in the context of divine judgment. It describes the action of destroying cities (Ezekiel 26:2), countries (Isaiah 37:18), idolatrous sanctuaries (Ezekiel 6:6), and sometimes the state that results from it ("desert," "desolate"). Very often, it is God who ravages — or God who allows to be ravaged — as punishment (Isaiah 42:15, Amos 7:9). Sometimes, it is human enemies who ravage (Judges 16:24: Samson ravaged Israel). The word always carries a connotation of total, irreversible, annihilating destruction.
H2717B.portee: This word confronts the believer with the reality of divine judgment: to ravage is not a trivial act, it is a total rupture, an end. It reminds us that God does not indefinitely tolerate evil and idolatry, and that desolation is the fruit of unfaithfulness. At the same time, it invites the believer to repent before being "ravaged," and to place his hope not in things that can be ruined, but in the God who judges and restores.

sens: To strike mortally, to take life by violence
To fight by shedding blood
To massacre, to destroy mercilessly
H2717C.detail:
1. The most common meaning: to cause someone to die by a violent blow, often with a sword. In 2 Kings 3:23, the kings "drew the sword" against each other and "struck one another" — a bloody battle between enemies.
2. The word describes the act of fighting with deadly intent, an armed confrontation where blood is shed. It is the harsh reality of war.
3. In a context of divine judgment, it means to destroy, to annihilate without mercy. In Jeremiah 50:21, God commands to "massacre" the rebellious inhabitants, and in Jeremiah 50:27, to "kill" the bulls — acts of complete extermination, without sparing.
H2717C.origine: The Hebrew root חרב (cha-rav) evokes the action of striking, of bringing down. It belongs to the family of verbs of attack and destruction. The word carries the image of the sword that falls, of violent combat. In the Hebrew Old Testament, this verb primarily expresses death inflicted by brute force, in war or in judgment.
H2717C.emploi: This verb appears 3 times in the provided usages, all in contexts of confrontation or judgment. In 2 Kings 3:23, it is a battle between kings where each strikes the other. In Jeremiah 50:21 and 50:27, it is the divine order to exterminate Babylon and its cattle — a judgment without remission. The word always describes an actively inflicted death, often collective, and carries particular gravity when it is the execution of a divine sentence.
H2717C.portee: This word reminds the reader of the harsh reality of violence and judgment. It does not soften it: when God commands to "crush" His enemies, the text does not hide that it is about death and destruction. This invites the believer to take divine justice seriously and the call not to rebel against God, whose judgment is irrevocable.

sens: To make a city or region uninhabitable, to leave it in ruins
To be ravaged, annihilated by war or misfortune
H2718.detail:
1. The verb evokes the action of reducing a city to a state of desolation: it is a destruction that renders it unusable and lifeless. In Ezra 4:15, it is said of Jerusalem that it "has been destroyed" — meaning the city had fallen into ruins, once inhabited and prosperous, now abandoned and devastated.
2. More broadly, the word can express the idea that an entire region is ravaged, stripped, annihilated by forces of destruction — destruction that can be the result of war, divine judgment, or political and economic decline.
H2718.origine: This Hebrew verb comes from a root that evokes the image of drying up and desolation. The central idea is that of something that is emptied of its substance, reduced to nothing, collapsing and ruining. This root is related to other Hebrew words denoting sterility and nakedness, the absence of life and fertility.
H2718.emploi: The word appears only once in the biblical text of the Segond, in Ezra 4:15. It is used in a letter addressed to the Persian king to warn him: it is argued that Jerusalem is a "destroyed city," a once powerful city now in ruins, capable of revolt, and therefore dangerous to royal power. This context shows that the word evokes a state of abandonment and ruin into which a prestigious city has fallen.
H2718.portee: This word reminds us that the kingdoms and cities of the world, no matter how great they may be, can be reduced to nothing and become ruins. It is a recurring biblical image: human greatness is not stable, and only the reign of God remains unshakable. For the believer, this invites reflection on the vanity of earthly constructions and the importance of seeking first the Kingdom of God.

sens: Combat weapon: a metal blade fixed to a handle, used in close combat.
Instrument of death and destruction in war.
Divine judgment or punishment sent by God.
Separation, division, rupture.
H2719.detail:
1. The sword is primarily the classic weapon of combat in antiquity: a sharp blade fixed to a handle. It is drawn, brandished, and strikes the enemy. Genesis 3:24 shows the cherubim wielding a flaming sword to guard access to the tree of life: it is a fearsome weapon, a symbol of divine protection.
2. In war, the sword is the instrument by which the greatest number falls: "Barak pursued the chariots and the army as far as Harosheth-Goim; and all the army of Sisera fell by the edge of the sword" (Judges 4:16). The edge or blade of the sword is spoken of, which kills mercilessly.
3. In prophecies, the sword becomes the symbol of God's judgment. When Jeremiah says, "we have been consumed by the sword and by famine" (Jeremiah 44:18), he speaks of the divine punishment that falls upon the unfaithful people. Ezekiel announces: "They will draw the sword against Egypt" (Ezekiel 30:11), and this sword is the instrument of God's vengeance.
4. Sometimes the sword represents separation and division: it cuts, it separates, it divides. It is an image of rupture and conflict in human relationships.
H2719.origine: The Hebrew word חֶרֶב (chérev) comes from a root that expresses the idea of burning, of drying up. The sword burns, it destroys, it consumes. That is why the word can also denote drought or dryness: the edge of the sword acts like fire that devours. The Hebrew cognates related to this root evoke heat and destruction. It is a very ancient word, attested in all biblical texts from Genesis onward.
H2719.emploi: The word "sword" is one of the most frequent words in the Hebrew Bible, with about 372 occurrences. It is found everywhere: in battle narratives (Joshua, Judges, 1 Samuel), in the laws (Exodus, Leviticus, Deuteronomy), and especially in the prophets (Jeremiah, Ezekiel, Isaiah). In the literal sense, it is the weapon of combat, often opposed to peace. Leviticus 26:6 promises: "I will give peace to the land," which implies the absence of the sword. In the figurative and religious sense, the sword is God's judgment and punishment: it does not act alone, but executes divine justice. Finally, the sword can denote any sharp or deadly instrument: knife, dagger, or even stone tools (Exodus 20:25 forbids working the stone of the altar with a sword).
H2719.portee: For the believer, the sword reminds us that God is judge, and that His judgment is inevitable: one should not provoke it. It also symbolizes divine protection when it is in the hands of God or His servants: it defends the righteous and strikes God's enemies. Finally, it invites meditation on violence and its causes: the Bible does not glorify the sword for itself, but sees it as the weapon of wars imposed by divine justice. It is a call to peace and obedience to God.

sens: Devoid of moisture, of water
H2720A.detail: 1. Lacking moisture, liquid. The "dry" bread of Proverbs 17:1 is bread without sauce or fat, contrasting with the abundance of juicy meats: it is simple, stripped food. The "dry" offering of Leviticus 7:10 is a pastry kneaded with oil that has not been soaked in sauce or additional liquid, thus easier to preserve and share.
H2720A.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root designating dryness and desiccation. It is the direct opposite of wet or moist: it evokes everything that has lost the water or liquid that characterized it. The same root appears in other Hebrew forms to describe dry land or a dried-up spring.
H2720A.emploi: The word appears twice in the Bible in Hebrew with this concrete sense of absence of moisture. In both cases, it qualifies food: bread without sauce (Proverbs 17:1) and an offering without additional liquid (Leviticus 7:10). These usages show that the word simply designates the material quality of a food item, not its taste or nutritional quality. Biblical wisdom contrasts dry bread with wealth, suggesting that poverty with peace surpasses abundance with quarrels.
H2720A.portee: This word invites reflection on true goods. The contrast in Proverbs 17:1 teaches that peaceful relationships are worth more than material prosperity and sumptuous feasts. A "dry morsel" with peace becomes an image of what truly matters: it is not external abundance, but the tranquility of the heart.

sens: Ravaged, in ruins, uninhabitable
Empty of inhabitants and life
Desolate, deprived of all resources
H2720B.detail:
1. The word first describes a city or wall that is completely destroyed, reduced to unusable ruins. Jerusalem after the Babylonian siege is an example: "Jerusalem is destroyed, and its gates are burned with fire" (Nehemiah 2:17). This is the physical state of destruction.

2. It then designates a place that has become empty and silent, without inhabitants or animals, thus without human or animal life. The prophet Jeremiah speaks of a time when these places are "desolate, without men or beasts" (Jeremiah 33:12), highlighting the disheartening contrast between a place created for life and its absolute silence.

3. The image extends to the idea of a land impoverished, sterile, deprived of its resources. The context of divine judgment in Haggai shows houses "in ruins" facing the neglected house of God (Haggai 1:4, 1:9), suggesting not only physical destruction but also economic and spiritual exhaustion.
H2720B.origine: The Hebrew word חָרֵב (cha.rev) literally means "dry," evoking the image of land, water, or a plant that has lost all moisture and vitality. It comes from a root that expresses the idea of drying and withering. This image of desiccation fits perfectly with urban ruins: a destroyed city is like a body deprived of its breath and life. In Greek, this word is often translated by terms expressing desolation and sterility.
H2720B.emploi: The word appears 8 times in the Hebrew Bible, mainly in the prophetic and post-exilic historical books. It primarily applies to Jerusalem after its destruction in 586 BC: Nehemiah reports it in his account of reconstruction (Nehemiah 2:3, 2:17). The prophets Jeremiah and Ezekiel use it to describe the state of divine judgment and the hope of restoration (Jeremiah 33:10, 33:12; Ezekiel 36:35, 36:38). Haggai uses it to reproach the neglect of the house of God (Haggai 1:4, 1:9). The word thus encompasses an entire era of national crisis: destruction, exile, and then the hope of reconstruction and repopulation.
H2720B.portee: This word reminds the reader of the reality of divine judgment on sin: disobedience leads to ruin and desolation. But the Bible does not leave this dark picture alone: it systematically shows that God can restore what was destroyed and give life to what was desolate. For the Christian, it is an assurance that no state of spiritual ruin is final if repentance and faith follow.

sens: the absence of moisture, the dry state
the absence or lack of water
the intense heat of the sun that dries up
the lack of rain or watering
H2721A.detail:
1. Drought first designates the state of what is dry, devoid of moisture. Gideon asks God for a sign: that the fleece remains dry while the ground is covered with dew (Judges 6:40).
2. It can more broadly refer to the absence or lack of water: Job says that his bones "dry up" (Job 30:30), the water retreats as if it evaporates.
3. The word also evokes the intense, burning heat of the sun that deprives the air and the earth of moisture. Jacob recounts how "the heat consumed me by day" (Genesis 31:40); Isaiah speaks of "a shelter from the heat of the day" (Isaiah 4:6).
4. Finally, it designates the lack of rain or watering, the deprivation that renders the land barren: Haggai announces that "drought will strike the land" (Haggai 1:11).
H2721A.origine: The Hebrew word חֹרֶב (horev) comes from a root that literally means "to burn" or "to be dry." It describes the drying action of the sun's heat. This word has also become the name of the desert of Sinai (Horeb, "the burning mountain"), where Moses encountered God near the burning bush — a desert where extreme drought prevails.
H2721A.emploi: The word appears 11 times in the Hebrew Bible, mainly to describe a painful physical condition or a natural phenomenon. Genesis 31:40 uses it for the heat of the day that oppresses Jacob. Judges 6:37-40 relates it to the absence of dew on the fleece — a visible contrast with the wet ground. Job 30:30 uses it figuratively: Job's bones dry up under suffering. Isaiah 4:6 and 25:4-5 place it in a context of divine deliverance: God offers shelter from heat and drought. Jeremiah and Haggai associate it with judgment: drought strikes as a consequence of unfaithfulness (Jeremiah 36:30; Haggai 1:11).
H2721A.portee: Drought in the Bible symbolizes trial, suffering, and sometimes divine judgment, but also the opportunity to see God's deliverance. For the Christian, this word reminds us that God notices our difficult conditions — as He saw Jacob's unbearable heat — and that He can offer us shelter and refreshment. It invites us to recognize our dependence on God for our most essential needs.

sens: State of ruin and abandonment after destruction
Destruction and ravage of a city or country
Loss, solitude, deep desolation
H2721B.detail:
1. Devastation describes a state of ruin where everything is destroyed and abandoned. When rebuilding on old ruins, one sees cities "devastated" for a long time, that is, reduced to rubble (Isaiah 61:4). This is the visible result of destruction.
2. It is the act of ravaging and completely destroying a city or country. God declares that Bozrah will become an "object of desolation, devastation, and curse" (Jeremiah 49:13), struck so deeply that it will not rise again. This is the punishment of divine judgment.
3. Figuratively, devastation evokes absolute solitude and the absence of life. When one sees flocks lying in the midst of a city, with only the cries of birds (pelicans) resounding where men once lived, "devastation" reigns: everything has become empty, bleak, without humanity (Zephaniah 2:14).
H2721B.origine: The Hebrew word חֹרֶב comes from a root that means "to be dry, burned." Devastation is a territory rendered sterile and dry like a desert, emptied of all life and greenery. This image of desiccation can describe both a natural drought and a war destruction: in both cases, the land becomes like a desert.
H2721B.emploi: The word devastation appears 4 times in the Greek New Testament to translate the Hebrew. It is mainly used for God's judgments on nations: Bozrah (Jeremiah 49:13), Egypt (Ezekiel 29:10), and the great city Nineveh (Zephaniah 2:14). Each time, the context shows a destruction so total that even the beasts and birds dominate the ruins. In Isaiah 61:4, on the contrary, the prophet promises future restoration: they will rebuild where devastation currently reigns. The word always marks a moment after destruction: it does not speak of the battle itself, but of what remains after.
H2721B.portee: This word reminds the reader that God's judgment is real and serious: a nation that refuses it does not become prosperous despite itself; it becomes a desert. But Isaiah 61:4 gives hope: even on the oldest ruins, God raises a people and restores what was lost. For the Christian, it is a promise that nothing is definitively destroyed when one turns to God.

sens: mountain of the desert of Sinai where God gave the Law to Moses
place of the theophany and the covenant between God and Israel
symbol of God's presence and His legislative authority
H2722.detail: 1. Horeb is a mountain located in the desert of Sinai, also called the "mountain of God" (Exodus 3:1). It is there that Moses was tending the flock when he encountered God in the burning bush. 2. This place is especially famous as the setting where God established His covenant with Israel and gave him the Ten Commandments inscribed on stone tablets (Deuteronomy 5:2). The entire nation gathered there, and many feared they would die upon hearing the divine voice and seeing the fire of judgment (Deuteronomy 4:10; 18:16). 3. In Israel's memory, Horeb becomes the very symbol of divine Law and God's absolute authority, to the point that the prophet Malachi, at the end of the Old Testament, calls the Israelites to remember "the Law of Moses" given at Horeb (Malachi 4:4).
H2722.origine: The Hebrew name חֹרֵב (Horeb) literally means "desert" or "desolation," which describes the arid and rocky landscape of the place. This same mountain is also called Sinai (סִינַי, Sinai, H5514), and both names refer to the same mountain: Horeb emphasizes its desert environment, while Sinai may derive from a root meaning "thorn" or refer to the thorny bush where God manifested Himself to Moses. Both terms are used interchangeably in biblical accounts.
H2722.emploi: Horeb appears 17 times in the Hebrew Bible, primarily in Exodus and Deuteronomy, at key moments of divine revelation. In Exodus, it is the site of God's first manifestation to Moses (Exodus 3:1) and the giving of the Law (Exodus 17:6). Deuteronomy repeatedly revisits this foundational event: Moses reminds the people that it was at Horeb that God spoke and established the covenant (Deuteronomy 1:6; 5:2), that it was there they feared death in the presence of the divine fire (Deuteronomy 4:10; 18:16). Later, the prophet Elijah goes to Horeb to seek God (1 Kings 19:8), and the tablets of the covenant rest there in the Temple (1 Kings 8:9). Horeb is thus the place where the relationship between God and His people was established through the Law and the covenant.
H2722.portee: For the Christian reader, Horeb symbolizes the moment when God revealed Himself in His demanding holiness and legislative justice. It is also the place where the covenant was established—a relationship of obedience and fear. The constant allusions to Horeb in Deuteronomy invite reflection on the nature of divine commandments and the responsibility of God's people to keep them. Finally, Horeb reminds us that encountering God is a daunting and transformative experience, producing both fear and obedience.

sens: A destroyed place, ravaged, where only the remains of buildings survive
An empty, abandoned, uninhabited area
The state of desolation of an entire city or region
The destruction itself, devastation as punishment
H2723.detail:
1. A ruin is primarily a physical place where destruction is visible: collapsed walls, debris (Isaiah 61:4: "they shall rebuild the old ruins, they shall raise up the former desolations"). It is the concrete result of devastation.
2. The word also designates the resulting space: an area that has become deserted, uninhabitable, where there is no longer any civil life (Leviticus 26:31: your cities shall become "desolations").
3. It evokes the state of an entire region struck by misfortune: when God says He will make Edom a "desolation," it is the whole country that will be emptied of its inhabitants and life (Ezekiel 25:13).
4. Finally, the word refers to the destructive act itself, to punishment: God "reduces" cities to ruins (Jeremiah 27:17), it is not an accident, it is a judgment.
H2723.origine: The Hebrew word חׇרְבָּה comes from a root meaning "to become dry, to become desolate." It is related to חֶרֶב (sword), as ruin can result from war, and to חׇרֵב (which means "dry, desert"). The underlying image is that of a land deprived of life: dry, abandoned, barren. In Greek, this word is generally translated as ἐρημία (eremia), which also carries the idea of desolation and emptiness.
H2723.emploi: The word appears 42 times in the Old Testament, especially in the prophets of the captivity (Jeremiah, Ezekiel) and in restoration texts (Isaiah, Ezra). It is frequently used to announce punishment: God threatens to reduce Jerusalem and the temple to ruins if Israel disobeys Him (Leviticus 26:31-33, Jeremiah 25:9). But the word also appears in oracles of consolation: the ruins will be rebuilt, the abandoned cities will be repopulated (Isaiah 61:4, Ezekiel 36:33). It is a key word in the theme of judgment and restoration: destruction, then reconstruction by the grace of God.
H2723.portee: This word confronts the believer with the reality of divine judgment: sin has visible and material consequences, not just spiritual ones. But it also carries hope: the ruins are not permanent. Isaiah 61:4 announces that God will restore the ruins by His Spirit; it is a promise for those who have experienced exile, and beyond that, for every soul destroyed by sin that returns to God.

sens: Land or ground devoid of water, dried up
An area devoid of water where one can walk or move
H2724.detail: 1. The word primarily designates land, soil, or ground that has lost the water that covered or soaked it. It is the state of the ground after drainage or evaporation: in Genesis 7:22, it is the "dry land" from which the waters of the flood have disappeared, where living beings breathed before their death. 2. By extension, it refers to a path or space that has become passable on dry ground, without water. When Moses strikes the sea in Exodus 14:21, the Lord "dries up the sea"—He removes the waters and creates a passage where the Israelites walk "on dry ground" (Joshua 3:17). Similarly, when Elijah strikes the Jordan in 2 Kings 2:8, the waters "part" and the two prophets cross "on dry ground." It is the reverse miracle of the flood: instead of drowning, God dries up to open a way.
H2724.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root meaning "to become dry" or "to dry up." It refers to the elemental image of water disappearing: a waterlogged ground becomes solid and hard again. It is a simple and concrete word, very visual, often used to describe God's great acts over water and land.
H2724.emploi: The word appears 7 times in the Hebrew Bible, mainly in miracle accounts related to water. It is used for the flood (Genesis 7:22), the crossing of the Red Sea (Exodus 14:21), the crossing of the Jordan under Joshua (Joshua 3:17 and 4:18), Elijah's miracle at the Jordan (2 Kings 2:8), and a prophecy against Egypt (Ezekiel 30:12). In each case, it marks the dramatic contrast: where water reigned, the ground becomes accessible. It is a key word for narrating how God masters the elements and creates a passage for His people.
H2724.portee: This word invites the reader to recognize God's power over creation. Each time the Lord "dries up" a sea or a river, He manifests His absolute sovereignty over water—the element that separates and engulfs—to save His people. It is a sign of deliverance: the dry ground becomes a path of liberation. These miracles remind the believer that no obstacle, however insurmountable it may seem, is beyond the reach of Him who commands nature.

sens: lack of water, absence of rain
drying up of the body or vigor
physical or moral exhaustion
H2725.detail:
1. Drought is primarily the prolonged absence of rain and water: a climatic state that dries up springs and scorches the earth. In Psalms 32:4, the psalmist speaks of his "vigor" reduced to the drought of summer, evoking vital energy dried up like soil deprived of water.
2. The word also designates the drying up of the body itself: when water is lacking for the living creature, it becomes exhausted, its strength fades away. The psalmist experiences this drought not because of the climate, but from the hand of God weighing upon him and consuming him.
3. Finally, it is an image of moral and spiritual exhaustion: the dried-up heart, the withered vigor, is the effect of sin, of guilt, before confession and forgiveness.
H2725.origine: The word comes from a root that means "to burn" or "to be burning." It literally describes the state of that which has lost all moisture: a sun-scorched soil in summer, land that does not receive rain. The image relates to the desert and aridity, which the Bible often associates with judgment or trial.
H2725.emploi: The word appears only once in the Bible, in Psalms 32:4. David confesses his hidden sin and the physical misery that resulted: his vigor had turned into drought, like grass that dies for lack of water. It is a moment of crisis before the grace of forgiveness, when the psalmist was still under the weight of unconfessed sin.
H2725.portee: This word reminds us that unconfessed sin affects not only the soul but also the body, the vital force, the energy of life. Drought also evokes spiritual exhaustion and the aridity of the heart far from God. It serves as an invitation to honest confession and to seek the living water that only God can provide.

sens: One of the seven eunuchs who served King Ahasuerus
H2726G.detail: 1. Harbona is one of the seven chamberlains or eunuchs serving King Ahasuerus (Xerxes) in Susa, the capital of the Persian Empire. He is specifically mentioned in Esther 1:10, among the palace officials responsible for conveying the king's orders and managing the affairs of his court.
H2726G.origine: The name Harbona (or Harbonah) literally means "the one who drives the donkeys" or "donkey driver," formed from Hebrew roots evoking the idea of transport and service. It is a name of Persian origin, attested only in the book of Esther, reflecting the context of the Persian Empire where the story takes place.
H2726G.emploi: Harbona appears only once in the Bible, in Esther 1:10. He is listed among the seven eunuchs of King Ahasuerus presented during a grand royal feast. His role was to ensure the communication of the sovereign's orders and to serve at court. He embodies one of the many official figures of the Persian palace, historical characters that are not detailed but essential to the administrative life of the court.

sens: Eunuch in the service of King Ahasuerus
One of the seven chamberlains of the royal court of Persia
H2726H.detail:
1. Harbona is a eunuch who served King Ahasuerus, meaning a court man directly attached to the service of the Persian monarch. His name literally means "donkey driver," which likely reflects an ancient task associated with servant duties.
2. He is among the seven trusted chamberlains or eunuchs surrounding the king. In this capacity, he had access to the inner palace and the ear of the sovereign, allowing him to report important information at the right moment.
H2726H.origine: The name Harbona means "donkey driver" or "the one who drives the donkeys." It designates a function of domestic servitude, typical of ancient royal courts. Its appearance in Persia reflects the customs of the court of King Ahasuerus, where eunuchs formed a trusted council around the monarch. The character appears only in the book of Esther and nowhere else in the Bible.
H2726H.emploi: Harbona appears only once in the entire Bible, in Esther 7:9. It is precisely at the moment when Haman, the enemy of the Jews, is arrested and judged by the king. Harbona's intervention at this critical moment shows his role as a confidant of the king: he reveals that Haman has prepared a gallows of fifty cubits to hang Mordecai, the Jew who saved the king's life. This denunciation accelerates Haman's death sentence and becomes the instrument of his downfall. Harbona thus symbolizes God's providential action, using even the servants of the palace to accomplish His justice.
H2726H.portee: Harbona's swift and decisive intervention illustrates how God acts in history, often in hidden ways, using circumstances and ordinary people to deliver His people. His courage to speak at the critical moment, without fear of Haman who was once all-powerful, shows that justice ultimately prevails. This character reminds the reader that God controls events and that no one, however high their position, can thwart His plan of salvation.

sens: To be shaken by a vibration, a movement
To be afraid, to be seized with fear
To show weakness in the face of danger
H2727.detail:
1. The verb first describes physical movement: to be agitated, to tremble, like something that vibrates. It is the concrete trembling of the body.
2. However, here, unlike a simple shiver, the trembling comes from fear: the enemies of Israel "tremble out of their fortresses" (Psalms 18:46), terrified by divine power and defeat.
3. This trembling reveals inner collapse: one who trembles is paralyzed by fear, losing strength and security — even entrenched in their strongholds, the king's adversaries cannot stand.
H2727.origine: The Hebrew verb חָרַג (charag) belongs to the family of words that describe abrupt and disturbed movements. The basic image is that of agitation, shaking: like when a building trembles, or when fear causes the body to vibrate. The context of Psalms 18 shows that it is always a trembling provoked by fear or adversity, never a normal movement.
H2727.emploi: The verb appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Psalms 18:46. It describes the reaction of foreign enemies in the face of the victory of the king (or the psalmist), strengthened by God. These adversaries, despite their fortifications, are seized with panic and terror: their trembling marks the helplessness of man before divine power. It is a rare word, but it expresses the major idea of the psalm: the superiority of the one whom God supports.
H2727.portee: To tremble in fear before God or danger is to acknowledge a power greater than one's own. For the believer, this passage affirms that those who oppose God and His people ultimately end up trembling and losing their assurance. It is a call to see God's hand at work in history and not to fear those who threaten God's people.

sens: edible jumping insect
creature capable of great leaps
clean animal according to Mosaic law
H2728.detail: 1. The word refers to a type of grasshopper or locust, an insect endowed with a great ability to jump. It is an animal commonly found in the Middle East and North Africa, capable of covering long distances by leaping. 2. The characteristic trait is its ability to jump: the Hebrew evokes the animal by its jumping movement, which defines it. 3. According to Leviticus 11:22, it is an animal that the Israelites could consume as clean: it was part of the legitimate menu for believers, unlike many prohibited insects.
H2728.origine: The Hebrew word חָרְגֹּל comes from a root that expresses the idea of jumping or leaping. The grasshopper is primarily identified as an animal by its ability to jump — it is the quintessential "jumper." This name defines it by its characteristic action, typical of Hebrew naming creatures by what they do.
H2728.emploi: The word appears only once in the Bible, in Leviticus 11:22, in the list of insects that the Israelites are allowed to eat. It is mentioned among other varieties of grasshoppers — the solam, the hargol, and the hagab — suggesting that it designates a particular species within the family of edible grasshoppers. The context is legislative and dietary: it serves to distinguish clean insects from unclean ones according to the Law.
H2728.portee: This word reminds us that the Mosaic Law was very practical and adapted to the real-life context of the Israelites: it even distinguished between varieties of insects based on their edibility, allowing for simple and affordable food — grasshoppers — while maintaining the boundaries between clean and unclean. It is a concrete detail of ancient piety.

sens: To tremble physically, to be shaken by involuntary movements
To be afraid, to be seized with fear or dread
To be disturbed, unsettled, thrown off balance
To cause trouble, to frighten someone
H2729.detail:
1. To tremble physically: the body shaken by an involuntary movement. The word primarily describes a visible trembling — that of a mountain at the feet of God (Exodus 19:18), or that of a person who trembles all over. It is the shudder that seizes someone who is surprised or overwhelmed: when Jacob learns that his money has reappeared in Benjamin's sack, his heart "trembles" (Genesis 42:28).
2. To be afraid, to be seized with fear: trembling becomes a sign of terror. When Saul learns of the Philistine invasion, "he was afraid" (1 Samuel 13:7) — the Hebrew word describes an inner shiver. Boaz, surprised to find a woman at his feet at night, "was terrified" (Ruth 3:8).
3. To be disturbed, unsettled: no longer enjoying peace or rest. When God promises Jacob that there will be "no one to trouble him," it means that Israel will dwell securely, without threat (Jeremiah 46:27, Ezekiel 34:28). This is the opposite of tranquility.
4. To cause trouble, to frighten: to put someone into trembling. David says he wants to "frighten" King Saul while he is weary (2 Samuel 17:2). It is to inspire fear or panic, often military in nature.
H2729.origine: The Hebrew root חרד expresses the idea of vibration, of movement that seizes the whole body. It is close to the notion of sudden trembling — a shivering that results from fear or surprise. The word appears mainly in dramatic narratives or in divine promises: its usage reveals how the Bible speaks of emotional and physical disturbance as a single embodied reality.
H2729.emploi: The verb appears 39 times in the Old Testament, primarily in historical narratives, the prophets, and the psalms. It describes the terror of humans in the face of a sudden threat (Genesis 27:33, Ruth 3:8), the anguish before divine judgment (1 Samuel 28:5), but also the physical phenomenon: the earth trembles (Exodus 19:18), the birds flee (Jeremiah 7:33). God often uses this verb to promise the end of trouble: "there will be no one to trouble them" recurs as a refrain of hope (Jeremiah 46:27, Ezekiel 34:28, Zephaniah 3:13). In military contexts, it refers to the rout of a terrified army (2 Samuel 17:2).
H2729.portee: This word speaks of human vulnerability in the face of real threats and fear. But it also reveals the biblical promise: God can dispel all that troubles His people. When the Bible says "you will not be troubled," it offers not the absence of difficulties, but peace in the presence of God. It is an invitation to recognize our fragility and to find our tranquility in God.

sens: who trembles, who is afraid
who dreads something or someone
who venerates with respect and fear
H2730.detail: 1. The literal sense is that of physical trembling: fear causes agitation, a shiver within us. Gideon asks those who tremble with fear, those who are afraid of battle, to return home (Judges 7:3) — these are the soldiers lacking courage. 2. More broadly, the word designates one who dreads, who is anxious, who suffers from worry. When Eli hears about the disaster, his heart was anxious for the ark of God (1 Samuel 4:13) — he is consumed by a worried concern. 3. In a spiritual context, the word takes on a nuance of respect mixed with reverent fear. Those who tremble at the words of God or His commandments (Ezra 9:4; Ezra 10:3; Isaiah 66:5) are not terrified, but deeply respectful, aware of divine authority — this is the "fear of God" that animates the believer.
H2730.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that expresses trembling, vibration, shaking: the basic idea is physical and corporeal. The same root produces words to designate what causes fright or what quivers. It evokes the agitation of the body in the face of danger or majesty.
H2730.emploi: This word appears six times in the Hebrew Bible, mostly in contexts of personal or religious fear. In Judges 7:3, it qualifies the fearful soldiers.
