In 1 Samuel 4:13, it describes Eli's anxiety. Ezra uses it twice (9:4 and 10:3) to speak of those who seriously respect the words of God — these people are not cowards, but faithful ones whom the requirements of the Lord fill with reverence. Isaiah does the same (66:2; 66:5): those who fear the word of the Lord, who listen with respect, are precisely those on whom God looks favorably. The meaning thus evolves from ordinary human fear to religious veneration.
H2730.portee: This word teaches us that authentic fear of God is not servile fear, but a deep and conscious respect for His authority. It is a noble disposition of the soul: one who fears the word of God shows that he takes seriously what He says, that he honors it. For the believer, recognizing God's majesty while trembling a little — by standing humbly before Him — is a mark of wisdom, not weakness.

sens: Physical trembling or shaking of the body caused by fear
Great fright or intense terror
Vivid emotion of surprise or anguish
Deep fear before God or danger
Anxious eagerness, worried solicitude
H2731.detail: 1. The word primarily denotes a trembling of the body, a shiver that seizes someone in fear: in 1 Samuel 14:15, "terror spread through the camp," which paralyzes the enemies of Israel and throws them into disarray. 2. It also expresses a sudden great fright, a terror that invades the soul: Isaac in Genesis 27:33 was seized by a violent emotion upon discovering that he had blessed the wrong son, so great was the shock that troubled him. 3. It is a deep anguish that can seize the heart: the prophet in Isaiah 21:4 is tormented by terror that turns his nights into horror. 4. The word can also signify a respectful fear before God, as in Proverbs 29:25, where "the fear of man lays a snare" — an anxious worry in the face of others' threats. 5. Sometimes, it takes on the meaning of eagerness or solicitude: in 2 Kings 4:13, the Shunammite shows "eagerness" to serve Elisha, a diligence full of care.
H2731.origine: The word comes from the root חרד (charad), which evokes the idea of trembling or shivering in fear. It belongs to a family of Hebrew words that describe different nuances of fear: from physical trembling to soul anguish. The root expresses the convulsive movement of the body seized by terror, an instinctive reaction to danger or the unknown.
H2731.emploi: This word appears 8 times in the Old Testament, mainly to describe moments of crisis or revelation. It describes Isaac's trembling during a terrible discovery (Genesis 27:33), the terror that paralyzes an enemy army (1 Samuel 14:15), the anguish of prophets confronted with the divine word or impending calamities (Isaiah 21:4, Jeremiah 30:5). The word can also qualify a respectful fear (Proverbs 29:25) or, in a more peaceful context, an eager solicitude (2 Kings 4:13). Its usage is concentrated around moments of intense emotion, whether it be terror, surprise, or reverence.
H2731.portee: This word reminds the reader that fear can paralyze the soul and that only trust in the Lord protects against the anxiety of men (Proverbs 29:25). It also shows how divine revelation seizes the prophet and disturbs his rest, a spiritual reality that should not be minimized. Terror can be a legitimate reaction to the mysteries of God, but the believer is called to transform it into reverence rather than panic.

sens: stage in the desert where Israel camped during the Exodus
H2732.detail: 1. Harada is a place in the desert that the Israelites passed through during their exodus from Egypt. It is a simple stop on the long journey: they came there from the mountain of Schaphar and departed to head toward Makheloth (Numbers 33:24-25). The name means "fear" in Hebrew, perhaps because this place inspired fear in the desert travelers.
H2732.origine: The Hebrew name חֲרָדָה (charadah) literally means "fear" or "dread," but it designates a geographical location here. Biblical tradition has preserved this name for a stop along the route taken by the Israelites under Moses' leadership, without further explanation as to the reasons for this designation.
H2732.emploi: Harada appears only twice in the Bible, solely in the account of the stages of the Exodus in Numbers 33. This passage methodically enumerates all the places where the Israelites set up their camps, from the exodus from Egypt to their arrival at the border of Canaan. Harada is listed among these many stops, with no particular event reported at this location.

sens: Place of origin for two warriors in King David's army
H2733.detail: Harod is a place from which two of King David's thirty-seven elite warriors originated: Shammah and Elika, both referred to as "of Harod" in 2 Samuel 23:25. The name means "trembling" in Hebrew, and it is likely a spring or fountain. These two men are among David's "Mighty Men," his most valiant soldiers.
H2733.origine: The name Harod comes from a Hebrew root meaning "to tremble, to shiver." It designates a spring or water source, and it is the trembling of the water or perhaps the vibration of the waters that inspired this name. The same place is mentioned in the account of Gideon in Judges 7, where the fountain of Harod serves as a landmark for gathering the army.
H2733.emploi: Harod appears as a specific geographical location in Palestine. Two of King David's thirty-seven elite warriors are from there: Shammah and Elika. The Bible provides no details about this place, but it is a well-known and recognizable location for contemporaries. The context shows that it is a water source, as fountains were often gathering places and landmarks in arid lands.

sens: To become burning, to be consumed with inner heat (primitive physical sense)
To experience a sudden and intense anger
To enter into fury, to be dominated by violent rage
To feel irritation, bitterness, or annoyance
To have one's anger kindled against someone (used mostly of God)
To be irritated, displeased, offended by something
H2734.detail:
1. The word first evokes the physical sensation of fire burning, of heat rising: that is why translations speak of "kindling." Genesis 4:5 shows Cain who "was very angry" (literally: "his anger was kindled"), as if an inner fire consumed him.
2. It is a sudden and intense anger that explodes, not a cold grudge: it erupts suddenly and takes away the character's self-control. In 1 Samuel 11:6, the Spirit of God seized Saul and "his anger was greatly kindled" — he became capable of acts he would not have accomplished in cold blood.
3. When fury rises, it can become violent and destructive. Exodus 32:19 reports that Moses, seeing the golden calf, "his anger was kindled" and he broke the tablets of the Law.
4. The word also applies to simple irritation, annoyance: Genesis 30:2 shows Jacob irritated with Rachel, without extreme violence.
5. The anger of God is kindled against the sin and idolatry of the people (Exodus 32:11, Deuteronomy 6:15, 2 Kings 13:3). It is the classic biblical expression of God's justice in the face of evil.
6. The verb can also describe a person's irritation against another for an offense or affront (1 Samuel 18:8: Saul was angry with David out of jealousy).
H2734.origine: The root חרה (cha-rah) is formed on the image of heat and fire rising. In Hebrew, "to be well" and "to be hot" share a conceptual kinship — what burns is what "goes" in the opposite sense. The words from the same family חם (cham, "hot") and חום (choum, "heat") reinforce this primary image. In the Greek translation of the Old Testament, this verb is generally rendered by θυμόω (thymoô) or παροργίζω (parorgizô), both of which express passionate irritation or rising anger.
H2734.emploi: This verb appears about 88 times in the Old Testament, mainly in narratives and psalms. It describes the anger of isolated characters — Cain angry at the rejection of his offering (Genesis 4:5), Saul kindled with jealousy against David (1 Samuel 18:8) — but also that of God in response to the collective sin of Israel. Divine anger is omnipresent: it is kindled against idolatry (Exodus 32, Deuteronomy 6:15), rebellion (Numbers 11-12, Joshua 7), unfaithfulness. Throughout the Old Testament, the verb takes on an increasingly "theological" tone: it becomes the key word to describe the rupture between God and His people when Israel strays from the covenant. The psalms use it to invoke the justified anger of the Lord against Israel's enemies.
H2734.portee: This word teaches the Christian reader that anger is not inherently bad: it is a powerful internal reality that can be just or unjust depending on its cause. God's anger is never arbitrary, capricious, or cruel; it responds to sin, unfaithfulness, and idolatry. In contrast, human anger is often unreasonable — like that of Cain — and reveals our need for inner self-control. This verb also invites recognition that God does not remain indifferent to evil; His anger is a sign of His love for justice and His commitment to His covenant with His people.

sens: Desert station of the people of Israel during their wandering in the desert
Stopover on the journey to the Promised Land
H2735.detail: 1. Hor-Guidgad is a desert station where Israel stopped during its long journey after leaving Egypt. It appears in the list of stops in Numbers 33, which enumerates all the encampments of Israel throughout the desert until the plains of Moab.
H2735.origine: The name literally means "cave of Gidgad." It is a geographical desert location whose name reflects its topographical characteristic: a cave or hollow in the rocky terrain of the desert. The same place is also called Gudgodah in other biblical texts, using a slightly different form of the same name.
H2735.emploi: Hor-Guidgad appears twice in the Bible, only in Numbers 33, in verse 32 where Israel arrives from Bené-Jaakan, and in verse 33 where the people depart for Jothbatha. It is a simple stopover in the desert itinerary without any particular event recorded. It marks one of the many stages that punctuate the forty-year journey through the desert.

sens: Father of Uzziel, a craftsman who participated in the rebuilding of the wall of Jerusalem under Nehemiah
H2736.detail: Harhaja is a man about whom nothing is known except that he is the father of Uzziel, a craftsman (artisan working with gold and precious metals). His son Uzziel distinguished himself by participating in the rebuilding of the wall of Jerusalem that Nehemiah ordered after the return from exile (Nehemiah 3:8). The name Harhaja literally means "fear of the Lord" or "fear of Jehovah," a meaning that reflects the piety expected of a believer, although the Bible gives us no details about Harhaja himself.
H2736.origine: The name Harhaja is composed of two Hebrew elements: "har" (fear, reverential fear) and "Jah" (abbreviation of the divine name Jehovah). The name thus expresses an attitude of respect before God, characteristic of the theophoric names (names including the name of God) borne by the Hebrews. It is a name confessing faith in God.
H2736.emploi: Harhaja appears only once in the Bible, in Nehemiah 3:8. In this passage, he is mentioned only as the father of Uzziel, a craftsman who worked on the rebuilding of the wall of Jerusalem alongside other skilled workers, including Hanania the perfumer. His mention is brief and functional: it simply identifies Uzziel by his lineage and perhaps also recalls the continuity of artisan families in Jerusalem after the exile.

sens: String of pearls threaded together
Necklace or adornment of pearls
H2737.detail:
1. A string of pearls is a series of pierced pearls threaded on a string or cord, forming an adornment. In the Song of Songs, the poet describes the beauty of the beloved by comparing her neck to a string of pearls (Song of Songs 1:10): the graceful neck, adorned with these carefully aligned pearls, conveys elegance and splendor.
2. By extension, the word also refers to the necklace itself, the complete adornment formed by this string of pearls. It is a luxury item, a symbol of refined beauty and wealth, which only women of high rank could wear.
H2737.origine: The Hebrew word חָרוּז (charouz) comes from a root that evokes the idea of piercing or making holes — for to make a string of pearls, each pearl must first be pierced. The word is related to the action of threading, of arranging round objects on a string. It appears only once in the Hebrew Bible.
H2737.emploi: This word appears only once in the entire Hebrew Bible: in Song of Songs 1:10. The biblical poet describes the adornment of a beloved woman whose beauty shines, her neck adorned with strings of precious pearls. The context is one of praise for the beloved, where every detail of her adornment contributes to expressing her splendor. It is a specialized term, perhaps borrowed from the vocabulary of Eastern luxury, which is used only once.
H2737.portee: This image of carefully aligned pearls teaches how authentic beauty combines delicacy and harmony in order. For the Christian reader, it also evokes the purity and precious value of one who trusts in the Lord, adorned with divine grace like a string of pearls.

sens: Wild thorny plant that grows in abandoned places
Dense and invasive vegetation that covers a land
Sign of desolation and divine judgment
H2738.detail:
1. The thornbush is a wild plant covered in thorns, which grows naturally in fields and uncultivated land. It represents everything undesirable and difficult to traverse. In Job 30:7, the unfortunate hide and cry "among the bushes" and "under the thornbushes," showing that these are places of misery where the desperate seek refuge.
2. The thornbush also refers to invasive vegetation that takes over a land: in Proverbs 24:31, the lazy man's field is covered with thornbushes that "cover its face," transforming a cultivated space into an impassable desert.
3. In a broader sense, the thornbush symbolizes desolation and the judgment of God. In Zephaniah 2:9, Moab and the children of Ammon will become "a place covered with thornbushes," an image of divine punishment that transforms a once-inhabited land into a barren and abandoned desert.
H2738.origine: The Hebrew word חָרוּל (charul) designates a thorny plant, probably a variety of thornbush or thistle. The image is that of hostile and invasive vegetation, which grows where nothing is maintained. This term always evokes abandonment, negligence, or judgment: a land without a master quickly becomes a tangle of thornbushes.
H2738.emploi: The word appears three times in the Hebrew Bible, always to evoke a situation of ruin or suffering. In Job 30:7, it is the refuge of the miserable who have lost their dignity. In Proverbs 24:31, it is the visible consequence of laziness and neglect: nature reclaims its rights and invades what was orderly. In Zephaniah 2:9, it is the instrument of God's judgment on the nations hostile to Israel. In each case, the thornbush marks the absence of care, of cultus, and therefore of organized life.
H2738.portee: The thornbush reminds us that abandonment and negligence have visible consequences: a life without direction, a neglected relationship with God, quickly becomes a barren tangle. It is also an image of God's judgment which, when it strikes a nation, removes all prosperity and security. For the reader, it invites cultivating one's spiritual life diligently, rather than allowing it to be overrun by disorder and sin.

sens: man of Judah at the time of restoration after the exile
H2739.detail: Harumaph is a Jewish man mentioned only once in the Bible, at the time when the people return from captivity in Babylon. He is the father of Jedaja, who participated in the rebuilding of the wall of Jerusalem under Nehemiah's direction (Nehemiah 3:10).
H2739.origine: The Hebrew name Harumaph literally means "split nose" or "torn nose," formed from two elements: "har" (mountain, or figuratively something prominent) and "umaph" (split, divided). It is a name characteristic of the time of the return from exile, when the Jews resumed their activities and their genealogies were recorded.
H2739.emploi: Harumaph appears only once in the Bible, in Nehemiah 3:10, in the list of builders who rebuilt the wall of Jerusalem. He is identified there as the father of Jedaja. This mention is part of the historical account of the Jewish people's return from captivity and the restoration of Jerusalem under Nehemiah, about 445 years before Christ. His inclusion in this list shows that he was a man of some importance in the community of Judah at this crucial moment in Jewish history.

sens: Burning intensity of anger
Violent and destructive manifestation of divine rage
Extreme emotional heat expressing wrath
H2740.detail:
1. The word describes anger not as a fleeting feeling, but as a burning, consuming force that devours the one who experiences it — like fire that consumes. In Exodus 15:7, Moses celebrates how God "unleashes Your anger," and this anger "consumes them like stubble," illustrating the image of destruction by fire.
2. This anger is always that of God in the Bible. It never refers to ordinary human irritation. It is His reaction to sin: it manifests through judgment, the ruin of cities and peoples. In Jeremiah 4:26, the cities are "destroyed before the Lord, before His burning anger," as if the anger itself were a destructive force accompanying divine judgment.
3. The word also evokes the urgency to flee: in Jeremiah 51:45, the people are called to "come out of her," to "escape from the fierce anger of the Lord," so great is this fervor and immediacy. It is a burning anger that does not leave one indifferent, that compels a response.
H2740.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root meaning "to burn" or "to be hot." It belongs to the same family as words evoking heat, fervor, and fire. This image of fire to express divine anger is common throughout the Bible: God's anger "burns" against sin, it consumes and destroys like flames. It is not a cold or distant anger, but a living, burning force, present.
H2740.emploi: This word appears 40 times in the Old Testament, almost exclusively to describe God's anger. It is found in the most serious contexts: after idolatry (Numbers 32:14), in the face of broken covenants (Deuteronomy 13:17), during prophetic judgments (Jeremiah, Ezekiel). The Psalms use it to celebrate or fear this divine anger. Ezra, Nehemiah, and the Chronicles use it to call the people to repentance, so that God's "fierce anger" may "turn away" (Ezra 10:14). The word does not vary much: it always retains this destructive fervor, this divine heat that ignites against evil.
H2740.portee: Understanding this fervor of anger invites the believer to take seriously the holiness of God and the weight of sin. It is not a capricious emotion, but a just and fearsome reaction to injustice. It also teaches that repentance is urgent: as long as this fervor has not turned away, judgment remains. For the Christian, this divine anger — fully poured out on Christ at the cross — becomes a reason for gratitude and obedience.

sens: Inhabitant of a locality called Haruph or Hariph
H2741.detail: Haroph refers to a man from a town named Haruph (or Hariph in Hebrew). It is an ethnic name indicating the geographical origin of a person, similar to saying today "Parisian" or "Lyonnais." In 1 Chronicles 12:5, a man from this clan, likely a warrior, is mentioned among those who came to join David at Ziklag.
H2741.origine: The word comes from the name of the locality Haruph (or Hariph), the precise etymology of which remains uncertain. In ancient Hebrew, forming an ethnic name from a city was common: a suffix was added to indicate belonging to that place. Haruph itself was probably a small town or village, but its exact location is not definitively identified in biblical geography.
H2741.emploi: Haroph appears only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 12:5. The context is during the time when David, fleeing from King Saul, gathers at Ziklag with his supporters. Several mighty men and warriors come to join him from various regions of Israel. This man from Haroph is among those fighters who support David in adversity, showing that his rallying attracted warriors from all over the land.

sens: Having a sharp point, cutting
Acting with zeal and application, eager in work
H2742A.detail:
1. In a physical sense, the word describes something that is pointed and sharp, capable of piercing or cutting. In Job 41:21, speaking of Leviathan, it describes "sharp points" under its belly, like formidable weapons.
2. In a moral and practical sense, it refers to one who works vigorously and without slackening, who is not lazy. Proverbs 10:4 contrasts the slack hand of the lazy with the hand of the "diligent" that enriches; Proverbs 13:4 states that the soul of the "diligent" will be satisfied, while the lazy cannot fulfill his desires.
H2742A.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root expressing the idea of point, sharpness, and liveliness. The primary image is that of a sharp and hard object. It has naturally been applied to the character of one who acts with liveliness and clarity, without slackness — like a sharpened tool that does not lag.
H2742A.emploi: The word appears about 10 times in the Hebrew Bible, mostly in Proverbs (six occurrences), but also in Job and among the prophets. In Proverbs, it characterizes the man who succeeds materially because he works hard and without hesitation: his plans lead to abundance (21:5), he will dominate (12:24), he will be satisfied (13:4). In Job 41:21 and in prophetic texts (Isaiah 28:27, 41:15, Amos 1:3), it describes sharp or cutting objects as traits of a formidable weapon or agricultural tools. The word always retains a nuance of activity, strength, and effectiveness.
H2742A.portee: For the reader of Proverbs, this word offers a clear vision of success: it comes from diligence in work, not from luck. The diligent enrich, accumulate, and succeed in their endeavors. It is a practical word of wisdom that encourages the believer not to yield to laziness, but to act with determination and care in their daily responsibilities.

sens: Decisive decision, final ruling
Verdict pronounced with authority
Moment of divine sentencing
H2742B.detail:
1. The word denotes a definitive and unappealable decision, rendered with force and clarity. It is a judgment that cuts, separating good from evil, without ambiguity. In Joel 3:14, "the valley of judgment" is the place where God renders His irrevocable sentence: "the multitude, a multitude, in the valley of judgment; for the day of the Lord is near, in the valley of judgment." 
2. This term emphasizes the authority and gravity of the one who judges: it is not an opinion or doubt, but a word that is fulfilled. Divine judgment is firm, enforceable, like a royal decision that cannot be revoked.
H2742B.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that evokes the idea of cutting, deciding clearly, separating. This image of clarity and firm decision is at the heart of the term: a judgment that separates, that distinguishes, leaving no room for doubt or negotiation. The root also carries the idea of diligence, promptness in execution.
H2742B.emploi: The word appears only once in the Hebrew Old Testament, in Joel 3:14. It specifically denotes the eschatological judgment, that is, the final judgment that God will render on all nations in the valley of judgment on the day of the Lord. This unique occurrence underscores its theological importance: it is a term reserved for supreme divine judgment, at the moment when God exercises His absolute authority and definitively determines the fate of humanity.
H2742B.portee: This word reminds the believer that God's judgment is neither hesitant nor unjust: it is a firm and definitive decision. It invites the fear of God and obedience, recognizing that there is a day when every act will be weighed. For those who place their trust in Christ, this certainty of divine judgment becomes an assurance: Jesus bore this judgment in our place.

sens: Trench dug in the ground, generally to delimit or fortify
Large depression or moat surrounding a fortified city
Figuratively: that which separates or distinguishes
H2742C.detail:
1. The word primarily refers to a trench intentionally dug into the ground, a linear excavation. In Daniel 9:25, the "ditches" of Jerusalem refer to the trenches or moats that surrounded and protected the city walls after its reconstruction; these are elements of a fortification, dug into the earth to strengthen defense.
2. More broadly, it is a deep depression, a pit or moat that marks a break in the terrain. These ditches were used in ancient times to hold water, create obstacles, or simply mark the boundaries of an urban or military enclosure.
3. Figuratively or metaphorically, a ditch can evoke that which separates, creating distance or distinction — although this usage is very limited in the Hebrew Bible.
H2742C.origine: The word חָרוּץ comes from a root that evokes the idea of digging, cutting, or dividing. It is formed on a verbal base expressing the action of digging or carving the earth. This word belongs to the vocabulary of fortifications and military architecture of the ancient Near East.
H2742C.emploi: The word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Daniel 9:25, in the context of the prophecy of the seventy weeks. It specifically refers to the ditches or moats of Jerusalem that are to be restored — rebuilt and reconstructed — after the Exile, as part of the city's rebuilding. The context is that of material and urban reconstruction, and the word emphasizes the defenses and fortifications of restored Jerusalem.
H2742C.portee: This word reminds us that the restoration of Israel after the Exile was not only spiritual but also concrete and material: the people had to rebuild their cities, their walls, and their defenses. For the reader, it illustrates how God fulfills His promises through visible and tangible historical events, and how the reconstruction of a people also involves the strength of its institutions and fortifications.

sens: The precious bright yellow metal, symbol of wealth and value
That which is precious and desirable, compared to gold in value
Wisdom and virtue, compared to gold for their pricelessness
H2742D.detail:
1. Gold is the most precious bright yellow metal, an object of wealth and desire. The psalmist evokes it in a poetic image: the wings of the doves covered with fine gold (Psalms 68:14).
2. This word also designates anything that is precious and desirable like gold, that which is cherished because it is rare and beautiful. Wisdom is better than gold: "For her acquisition is better than that of fine gold" (Proverbs 3:14).
3. By extension, it spiritually represents wisdom, instruction, and virtue, which surpass in value all material goods. "I would rather have wisdom than gold" (Proverbs 8:10 and 8:19), and "Better is wisdom than gold" (Proverbs 16:16).
H2742D.origine: The Hebrew word חָרוּץ (charuts) primarily refers to the metal gold by its bright color and malleability. It comes from a root evoking fineness and purity, as gold was refined and purified by fire, making it even more precious. In biblical poetry, this word often takes on a figurative meaning to denote anything of great value.
H2742D.emploi: This word appears six times in the Bible, almost exclusively in the poetic and wisdom books (Proverbs, Psalms) and once in the prophet Zechariah. It is never used neutrally to describe ordinary gold objects (jewelry, cups), but always in a poetic or comparative context: wisdom is better than gold (Proverbs 3:14, 8:10, 8:19, 16:16), or to evoke divine beauty (Psalms 68:14). The last occurrence (Zechariah 9:3) uses gold as a symbol of earthly wealth that God will overturn.
H2742D.portee: This word invites the believer to reevaluate their true riches. The Bible does not despise gold in itself, but it constantly calls to prefer wisdom, the fear of God, and virtue over material wealth. For the Christian reader, it is a reminder that true prosperity is not that of perishable treasures, but that of the knowledge of God and moral uprightness.

sens: Man from Jotbah, father of Mescullémeth
H2743.detail: Haruts is a minor character in the Old Testament, mentioned only once in the history of the divided monarchy. He is the father of Mescullémeth, who became the wife of King Manasseh of Judah and the mother of King Amon (2 Kings 21:19). His name appears in the royal genealogy, marking his descent in the line of the kings of Judah, even though he himself was just a man from the city of Jotbah, without apparent political power.
H2743.origine: The name Haruts literally means "zealous" or "diligent" in Hebrew, formed from a root that expresses eagerness and fervor in accomplishing something. Although its etymology is clear, the man himself remains enigmatic: the Bible tells us nothing about him except that he was from Jotbah and that he had a daughter who ascended the throne alongside a king of Judah.
H2743.emploi: Haruts appears only once in the Bible, in 2 Kings 21:19, at the moment when the historian notes the origins of the mother of King Amon. The mention of his name and his city indicates that, despite the absence of other biographical details, the maternal genealogy of the kings of Judah was carefully recorded to establish succession rights and family alliances. Haruts remains an example of those characters whose political role was limited, but whose descendants marked royal history.

sens: Head of a family among the Nethinim who returned from exile with Zerubbabel
H2744.detail: Harhur is a head of a family of Nethinim — servants of the Temple — who participated in the return of the exiles to Jerusalem after the Babylonian captivity, under the leadership of Zerubbabel in the sixth century B.C. His name appears in both official lists of those who returned: that of Ezra and that of Nehemiah, each recording the sons of Harhur among the descendants of the Temple servants (Ezra 2:51 and Nehemiah 7:53). These lists show that the entire returning community was duly accounted for and recognized in its religious function.
H2744.origine: The name Harhur literally means "inflammation" or "burning" in Hebrew. It is an uncommon name that likely characterized the person by remarkable ardor or brilliance. This Harhur is known only by these two parallel mentions in the return registers of the exile.
H2744.emploi: Harhur is mentioned only twice in the Bible, in the same verses of Ezra 2:51 and Nehemiah 7:53, where the parallel lists of families returning from Babylon with Zerubbabel around 538 B.C. are found. He is classified among the Nethinim, this special category of servants dedicated to the Temple. His name designates not only an individual but also his descendants: "the sons of Harhur" will continue the service of the Temple after the return. These two identical mentions show the importance given to these records in the restoration of the Jewish community.
H2744.portee: The mention of Harhur reminds us that the return from exile involved all the servants of the Temple, not just the priests and Levites. It shows that God did not forget those who, even in the humblest roles, belonged to His people and His worship. For the Christian reader, it is a sign that God cares for each individual and integrates them into His restoration plan, regardless of their position.

sens: Grandfather of Shallum, husband of the prophetess Huldah
H2745.detail: Harhas is a man from the time of the divided monarchy, mentioned only once in the Bible. He is the father of Tikvah and the grandfather of Shallum, who was the husband of Huldah, the prophetess consulted by King Josiah when the Book of the Law was discovered in the Temple (2 Kings 22:14). The biblical text refers to Harhas as the "keeper of the garments" of the Temple, indicating that he held an important position in the service of the Temple.
H2745.origine: The name Harhas literally means "very poor." Despite this humble meaning, the biblical text shows that Harhas was a person of respectable status, as his family was connected to the service of the Temple and his granddaughter was a recognized prophetess. His name may have been a nickname or reflect a particular circumstance in his life. The text of Chronicles also calls him Hasrah, a variant of the same name.
H2745.emploi: Harhas appears only once in the Bible, in 2 Kings 22:14, in the context of King Josiah's reign. He is mentioned solely as the grandfather of Shallum, indicating that this character had some notoriety in the family genealogy, without being a major actor in biblical history. His sole mention places him at the time of the discovery of the Book of the Law (late 7th century BC).

sens: Extreme and intense temperature
Inflammation or fever of the body
Destructive fervor
H2746.detail:
1. The "scorching heat" refers to an extreme and unbearable temperature, one that consumes and dries out. In Deuteronomy 28:22, it is listed among the plagues sent by the Lord: a heat that ravages the body as the sun burns the earth.
2. The word also evokes feverish inflammation, the intense fever that devours the organism. It is an internal, destructive heat that weakens and kills.
3. Figuratively, it is the image of a violent and devastating fervor, a power that consumes everything in its path — like divine anger that destroys mercilessly.
H2746.origine: The Hebrew word חַרְחֻר (char.chur) comes from the root חרר (harrar), which means "to burn" or "to be ardent." It is a reduplicated word: the repetition of the root intensifies the meaning and creates the idea of extreme and relentless heat. The reduplication mimics the effect itself: a heat that does not cease to burn.
H2746.emploi: This word appears only once in the Bible, in Deuteronomy 28:22, in the solemn context of the curses that the Lord promises to the Israelites if they disobey His covenant. The "scorching heat" is a concrete divine plague, an epidemic of fever and burning that decimates the people. It is part of a series of punishments: consumption, fever, inflammation, drying out, jaundice, and gangrene. This enumeration of ailments shows that the scorching heat is both a symptom of illness and a plague in itself.
H2746.portee: Even though this word appears only once, it reminds the believer that illness and suffering are not accidents of chance: they can be calls from God to return to Him and to obedience. The scorching heat symbolizes the intensity of divine judgment, its concrete reality. It is a warning: living according to God's commandments brings blessing, while rebellion leads to serious physical and spiritual consequences.

sens: Sharp instrument for engraving or marking
Action of engraving or marking
To trace quickly, to hurry
H2747.detail:
1. The word primarily refers to a sharp and pointed tool, such as a punch or chisel, used for engraving, carving, or marking a surface — for example, metal or stone. The image is that of the instrument that makes clear and deep marks.
2. By extension, it can also refer to the very action of engraving or tracing with this tool — the work done with the chisel. In Exodus 32:4, the word appears in the context of the making of the golden calf, where the molten gold is poured into a mold (literally "engraved" or "shaped").
3. In a more figurative or derived sense, the word takes on the meaning of haste or urgency — as if one were tracing quickly without taking time. In Isaiah 8:1, there is a call to hurry to plunder, meaning to act quickly and without delay.
H2747.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that evokes the idea of tracing, engraving, or digging. The engraving tool is the primary image: it is what engraves, what marks deeply. The idea of haste may derive from a semantic evolution where "to engrave quickly" becomes "to hurry" or "to act fast."
H2747.emploi: The word appears only twice in the Hebrew Bible. In Exodus 32:4, it refers to the mold or shaping of gold into a golden calf: Aaron receives the gold and melts it in a mold to form an idol. In Isaiah 8:1, the prophet is commanded to write on a tablet in such a way that they hurry to plunder — here the word carries more the sense of urgency or haste. The usage thus varies between the tool and the quick action.
H2747.portee: This word reminds us that every act of creation — including idolatry — requires tools and work. In Exodus, it highlights the human fabrication of the golden calf: it is not a god that falls from the sky, but an object shaped by human hands. In Isaiah, it reinforces the urgency of divine judgment on the nations: time is pressing, action is accelerating. For the believer, these two passages teach to be wary of human creations presented as divine, and to take seriously the haste of God's judgment.

sens: One who practices magic and occult arts in Egypt
Scholar or advisor to Pharaoh consulted to interpret signs and mysteries
One who claims to perform wonders through secret formulas or enchantments
H2748.detail:
1. The Egyptian magician is a practitioner of occult arts, someone who claims hidden knowledge about supernatural forces. When Pharaoh has a troubling dream, he first summons these magicians to interpret it (Genesis 41:8) — this is a political and religious act: one consults those believed to be in contact with the divine.
2. In the eyes of the Egyptians, the magician is also a wise man, a court advisor invested with particular authority. Pharaoh reports his dreams to him as to someone trustworthy (Genesis 41:24), hoping that this occult knowledge will unveil the mystery.
3. The magicians claim to perform signs and wonders through their enchantments. With each of the plagues, they attempt to replicate what God accomplishes through Moses: they bring forth frogs (Exodus 8:3) or work to produce lice (Exodus 8:14). But gradually, they admit defeat — unable to compete with the power of the Lord.
H2748.origine: The Hebrew word חַרְטֹם (chartom) likely comes from an ancient Egyptian root and literally means "one who engraves" or "one who writes" — alluding to sacred and hieroglyphic writing, associated in Egypt with esoteric knowledge. The word reflects the biblical image of an elite that is educated and mysterious. An identical Aramaic form exists in late Hebrew, showing that the term has persisted in the vocabulary of the Near East.
H2748.emploi: This word appears mainly in the story of the plagues of Egypt and in the accounts of Pharaoh's court (Genesis, Exodus, Daniel). It always designates the occult advisors of Pharaoh — those who are supposed to possess magical and esoteric knowledge. At the beginning of the plague cycle (Exodus 7:11; 7:22), they succeed in imitating Moses' wonders and thus lend credence to the idea that Pharaoh is in control of the situation. But starting from the third plague of lice (Exodus 8:14 to 8:15), they fail and must admit defeat. This narrative progression emphasizes that the Egyptian magicians, with all their reputed knowledge, can do nothing against the power of the true God. Daniel also encounters the magicians of Babylon (Daniel 1:20; 2:2) in a similar context: supposedly learned sages who discover their impotence in the face of the wisdom that God gives to His servants.
H2748.portee: This word reminds us that non-biblical civilizations place their trust in forms of wisdom and power that prove illusory or vain. It underscores how magic and the occult, however prestigious they may appear in the eyes of the world, remain powerless before the living God. It is an invitation not to seek true understanding and true power in hidden arts, but to recognize their emptiness.

sens: Specialist in occult arts and divination
One who claims to interpret dreams and mysterious signs
Advisor to the king consulted for supernatural matters
H2749.detail:
1. The magician is a man who claims knowledge of hidden arts, magic, and divination. In Mesopotamian royal courts, he was an official figure, consulted for questions that ordinary wisdom could not resolve. Daniel 2:10 shows the magicians of King Nebuchadnezzar declaring that no man on earth can do what the king demands — reveal and interpret a forgotten dream.
2. The magician was one who was asked to interpret dreams, visions, and omens. He was a diviner, an astrologer who claimed to read the supernatural. In Daniel 4:7, the magicians come with the astrologers and the Chaldeans, but they prove unable to explain the king's dream.
3. By extension, the magician could be a high official of the kingdom, head of a class of royal advisors. Daniel 4:9 shows Belteshazzar, chief of the magicians, to whom the spirit of the holy gods is attributed, capable of revealing the deepest mysteries.
H2749.origine: The Hebrew word חַרְטֹם (chartom) refers to one who practices the art of incantations, secret formulas, and divination. It is related to the idea of engraving, tracing mystical signs — like a scribe who writes magical formulas. The Aramaic term chartiom carries the exact same meaning. In pharaonic Egypt, these figures played a very similar role: they were the "priests" of magic and occult wisdom.
H2749.emploi: The word appears 5 times in Daniel, always in chapters 2 and 4-5, during the account of Nebuchadnezzar. The magicians form an official group at court, often mentioned alongside astrologers and Chaldeans (Daniel 2:27, 4:7, 5:11). They represent the wisdom of the pagan world, and the text systematically emphasizes their powerlessness in the face of divine visions that only Daniel, guided by the God of Israel, can interpret. In Daniel 4:9, Belteshazzar, the chief of the magicians, is distinguished by the king's recognition — but even he cannot solve the riddle of the dream without the intervention of Daniel and the God of Judah.
H2749.portee: This word reminds the reader that purely human wisdom, divination, and magic remain powerless against God's plans. The magicians of Babylon embody a false wisdom that ignores the true God. In contrast, Daniel — a young captive — reveals a superior wisdom because he trusts in the living God. For the believer, this contrast teaches that no hidden science, no occult power can rival the knowledge that God alone possesses and communicates.

sens: The burning anger that inflames someone, their intense rage
The visible and destructive manifestation of this anger, like a consuming fire
H2750.detail: 1. The word denotes anger in its most intense and burning dimension, as if it ignites the person from within. It is an anger that cannot be contained, that rises and consumes. Moses leaves Pharaoh in this "burning anger" (Exodus 11:8): he is seen leaving with a rage that is evident on his face and in his gestures. 2. Beyond the inner feeling, this word evokes anger that manifests outwardly, burning and destroying like fire. In Lamentations 2:3, it is in His "burning anger" that God cuts down the strength of Israel and ignites flames that consume: anger becomes a visible, palpable destructive force that ravages everything in its path.
H2750.origine: The word comes from a root meaning "to burn," "to be hot." The basic image is that of intense heat, of fire. The word always retains this dimension: anger is described as a heat that ignites, that consumes. This is why it is applied both to the feeling (the fervor that rises within us) and to its effects (the destruction it causes).
H2750.emploi: The word appears six times in the Old Testament, always to speak of intense and destructive anger. It applies to the anger of men (Moses in Exodus 11:8, Saul in 1 Samuel 20:34, the warriors of Ephraim in 2 Chronicles 25:10) and to that of God (in Deuteronomy 29:24 and Lamentations 2:3). In each case, this anger is presented as something serious, that acts, that produces effects: it drives to action, it destroys, it irritates. It is always anger at its most intense degree, one that cannot be contained.
H2750.portee: This word shows us that anger, even when justified (like that of Moses or God in the face of unfaithfulness), possesses a fearsome destructive power. It should not be provoked lightly. For the believer, this invites caution before one's own anger and reverence before God's anger, which judges with a justice that burns against evil.

sens: Bread of pale or light color, made with white flour
H2751.detail: 1. White bread is pale in color, obtained from higher quality flour. It is a more refined and expensive food than ordinary bread. In the dream of the chief baker, Joseph sees three baskets of white bread on his head, symbolizing the wealth and prosperity of Pharaoh (Genesis 40:16).
H2751.origine: The Hebrew word חֹרִי (chori) comes from a root meaning "white" or "pale." In biblical Hebrew, this root applies to what is light-colored or bright. White bread was a luxury product in ancient Egypt, reserved for the wealthy and important meals.
H2751.emploi: The word appears only once in the Bible, in Genesis 40:16. It is found in the dream of the chief baker in Egypt, while Joseph was imprisoned with him. This dream, interpreted by Joseph, announced the restoration of the chief to his position and his ability to serve Pharaoh again. The use of the term "white bread" emphasizes the quality and dignity of this royal service.
H2751.portee: This detail of the dream reminds us that God sometimes communicates with man through precise and symbolic images. For the reader, it shows how Joseph, guided by the Spirit, could interpret dreams and discern God's plans, even in prison. This ability will ultimately open the way for him to honor before Pharaoh.

sens: peoples and chiefs living in Mount Seir before Esau
descendants of Hor, contemporary of the patriarchs
H2752.detail:
1. The Horites are the original inhabitants of Mount Seir and the region of Edom. This people occupied these mountainous territories before the arrival of the descendants of Esau (Genesis 36:21, 36:29). They had their own chiefs and social organization.

2. Hor was a man who lived during the time of the patriarchs, ancestor of this people. The Horites derive their name from this founding ancestor. The word literally means "one who dwells in caves," perhaps evoking life in the mountainous regions and their natural caves of Mount Seir.
H2752.origine: The word comes from Hor (חֹרִי), a man from the time of the patriarchs. The name means "inhabitant of caves," revealing how this people was characterized: mountain dwellers living in the cavities of the terrain. This people, predating Esau, already occupied Mount Seir when the descendants of Esau arrived.
H2752.emploi: The Horites appear six times in the Bible, mainly in Genesis and Deuteronomy. Genesis 14:6 shows them in Seir during the time of Abraham. Genesis 36 lists their chiefs: Lotan, Shobal, Zibeon, and Anah. Deuteronomy 2:12 and 2:22 recount how the children of Esau drove them out and took their place, just as Israel took the promised land. They disappear from biblical history, replaced by the Edomites (descendants of Esau).
H2752.portee: The Horites remind us that God makes room for the peoples He has chosen: Israel received Canaan just as the Edomites received Seir. This change of population illustrates how God disposes of nations according to His purpose, making room for the heirs He has planned.

sens: Man of the tribe of Simeon, father of Shaphat
Name meaning 'one who dwells in a cave'
H2753G.detail: Hori is a man of the tribe of Simeon mentioned only once in the Bible, in Numbers 13:5. He is the father of Shaphat, whom Moses sends to scout the land of Canaan. His name, which literally means 'one who dwells in a cave,' may evoke a troglodyte dwelling or an ancestral origin linked to caves, a trait found in other peoples of that time.
H2753G.origine: The name Hori comes from an ancient Hebrew root meaning 'cave' or 'hole.' This same element is found in the name of the Horites (חֹרִים), a semi-nomadic people who lived in the mountains of Seir before the arrival of the Edomites. Although Hori is clearly a man of Simeon in Numbers 13:5, the same name appears elsewhere in the Old Testament to designate a Horite, son of Lotan and grandson of Seir, showing how this name was borne by different peoples in the region.
H2753G.emploi: Hori appears only once in the Bible, in Numbers 13:5. He is mentioned as the father of Shaphat, one of the twelve men Moses sends to explore the land of Canaan before entering the Promised Land. Shaphat represents the tribe of Simeon during this spying mission. This passage places Hori in a crucial moment in Israel's history, even though the Bible provides no further details about his life or role.

sens: Son of Lotan, one of the ancient inhabitants of the land of Edom
Inhabitant of the land of Seir, belonging to the people of the Horites
H2753H.detail:
1. Hori is a man living in the time of the Patriarchs, son of Lotan. He appears in the genealogy of the peoples of Edom, mentioned alongside his brother Hemam (Genesis 36:22). He is part of the ancient inhabitants of the region before the arrival of other peoples.
2. Hori represents the people of the Horites, these ancient inhabitants of the land of Seir (Edom). Genesis 36:30 lists the Horite chiefs, showing that they formed an organized community in this land before being supplanted by other peoples.
H2753H.origine: The name Hori (חֹרִי) literally means 'inhabitant of a cave' or 'one who dwells in a cave' (from חור, 'cave'). It is the same word that in Greek gives 'Horite' and in French 'Horiens.' This name likely reflects the lifestyle or type of habitat of this people in the mountainous regions of Edom.
H2753H.emploi: Hori is mentioned three times in Scripture, exclusively in the genealogies of Edom. Genesis 36:22 identifies him as the son of Lotan. Genesis 36:30 places him among the Horite chiefs of the land of Seir. The same man also appears in 1 Chronicles 1:39 in a similar genealogical recap. These mentions show that Hori was an important figure of the Horite people, notable enough to appear in the genealogical records preserved by Israel.
H2753H.portee: The mention of the Horites in the Bible reminds readers that God established the borders of nations long before Israel. These ancient, well-organized peoples ultimately yielded according to God's purposes. It is a lesson in humility about divine sovereignty over the history of nations.

sens: Small bag or purse used to carry and store small objects or money
Accessory of clothing worn suspended from the belt
H2754.detail:
1. The word refers to a small or medium-sized bag made of fabric or leather, intended to contain and transport valuable objects or money. In 2 Kings 5:23, Naaman fills two bags with silver (two talents) — a significant amount — which he entrusts to his servants, showing that this bag was sturdy enough to carry weight.
2. The word can also refer to a game bag, that is, a small bag or purse worn suspended from the belt as a clothing accessory. In Isaiah 3:22, it is listed among the precious adornments and ornaments of women — cloaks, tunics, game bags — indicating its role as both a practical and decorative accessory.
H2754.origine: The Hebrew word חָרִיט (charit) comes from a root evoking the idea of digging or chiseling, suggesting a crafted or shaped object. It is a made bag, not just a simple piece of cloth. The word belongs to the concrete vocabulary of everyday objects, particularly in commerce and the safeguarding of valuable goods.
H2754.emploi: The word appears only twice in the Hebrew Bible. In 2 Kings 5:23, in the context of Naaman's journey to Israel, it refers to the bags of silver — a practical and economic use. In Isaiah 3:22, it appears in a satirical enumeration of the luxurious adornments and accessories of the women of Jerusalem, criticized for their pride: here the bag takes on a value of adornment and social status. The word thus oscillates between a utilitarian object and a sign of wealth.
H2754.portee: This small word reminds us that in the Bible, the simplest objects — a bag, a purse — can carry spiritual weight: transporting Naaman's money without faith, or reflecting the vain pride of those who adorned themselves with luxury while judgment was approaching. It invites us to see that everything we possess and carry with us tells a story of the heart.

sens: Family chief returned from exile with Zerubbabel
Signatory of Nehemiah's covenant
H2756G.detail: Hariph is a man mentioned only once in the Bible, in Nehemiah 10:19. He was the head of a family among the exiles who returned from Babylon with Zerubbabel to rebuild Jerusalem after the captivity. His name appears in the official list of the leaders of the people who sealed the renewed covenant with God under Nehemiah's leadership, showing that he was a figure of responsibility and authority among the returning Jews.
H2756G.origine: The name Hariph means 'a tearing away' or 'a gathering,' evoking the idea of separating or detaching. It carries the image of a rupture or extraction, fitting for a man whose people had just been torn from Babylonian exile to return to Jerusalem.
H2756G.emploi: Hariph appears only once in the Bible, in Nehemiah 10:19. He is named among the family leaders who sign the renewed covenant with God during the return from exile. This unique mention shows his official role in the communal restoration of Israel after captivity, with no further details about his life or personal actions.

sens: Family chief of exiles returned from Babylon
H2756H.detail: Hariph is a family chief among the exiles who returned from Babylon to the Holy Land after captivity. His name appears in the list of leaders whose descendants participated in the return (Nehemiah 7:24), where it is noted that the sons of Hariph formed a group of one hundred twelve people.
H2756H.origine: The name Hariph (חָרִיף) literally means 'a tearing away' or 'a harvest' — the idea of removing or gathering. It is a speaking name, common among Jewish families of the Exile and Return period. The same character is also called Jorab or Jorah in other lists.
H2756H.emploi: Hariph is mentioned only once in the Bible, in Nehemiah 7:24, in the list of families that returned from captivity in Babylon with Zerubbabel. This list includes several family leaders and the number of their descendants, which helped document the reconstituted community. Hariph also appears in the list of signatories of the covenant made under Nehemiah's leadership (perhaps under another name), showing his commitment to the spiritual and political renewal of Jerusalem.
H2756H.portee: Hariph represents the ordinary family leaders who had the courage to leave the safety of Babylonian exile to return and rebuild Jerusalem and the Temple. His name reminds us that the return from exile was not led solely by great heroes, but also by faithful men whose families worked together for the restoration of God's people.

sens: Farming tool with teeth or sharp blades, intended to break up clods of earth
Sharp or serrated object used as an instrument of punishment or torture
H2757.detail:
1. The harrow is an agricultural tool equipped with teeth or sharp blades, dragged over the ground to break it up after plowing. It is a basic tool of ancient farming, allowing for soil preparation for sowing. The context of 1 Samuel 17:18 plays on this double meaning: cheese was once curdled and pressed into grilled or serrated molds, hence the image of a "harrow" of cheese.
2. The word also refers to a serrated and sharp instrument used for punishment or torture. In 2 Samuel 12:31 and 1 Chronicles 20:3, David puts the Ammonite inhabitants "under iron harrows," probably instruments of torture or sharp grids, an expression that signifies a violent punishment inflicted on the defeated. The term evokes here the serrated and cutting aspect of the tool.
H2757.origine: The Hebrew word חָרִיץ (cha-rits) comes from a root meaning "to cut, to slice, to sever." The primary image is that of incision, of a clean cut: the word is recognized in other Hebrew forms designating pointed or sharp objects. The harrow is named so because its teeth or blades cut and break the earth.
H2757.emploi: The word appears only three times in the Hebrew Bible. The first occurrence, in 1 Samuel 17:18, uses it in an agricultural or food-related sense (pressed cheese). The other two, in 2 Samuel 12:31 and 1 Chronicles 20:3 (parallel text), place it in a military and punitive context, among other instruments (saws, axes, brick kilns), suggesting a use of torture or punishment inflicted on the Ammonite prisoners of war. The meaning thus varies from a domestic tool to an instrument of torture.
H2757.portee: This word reminds us that the Bible does not hide the violent realities of ancient warfare and punishments of the time. For the modern reader, it invites us to look beyond moral judgment on these ancient practices: the Word of God records history without systematically justifying it, and the progressive teaching of mercy in Scripture shows a direction toward justice tempered by compassion.

sens: action of plowing, turning the earth with a plow
time of year when plowing occurs
agricultural work of preparing fields
set of agricultural tasks
H2758.detail:
1. Plowing is primarily the concrete action of turning the earth with a plow or sharp instrument: it is preparing the soil for sowing. In Genesis 45:6, during seven years of famine, there is neither plowing nor harvest — the land remains useless, barren.
2. The word also refers to the season, the time of year when this activity takes place. In Exodus 34:21, God commands to rest on the seventh day "even during the time of plowing and harvest" — meaning that the Sabbath rest is required even during the busiest agricultural periods.
3. By extension, plowing becomes synonymous with agricultural work, with what the farmer's effort produces. In 1 Samuel 8:12, the king requisitions young men to "plow his fields" — transforming a field into cultivable property.
H2758.origine: The Hebrew word חָרִישׁ (charish) comes from a root meaning "engraving, incision" — to plow is indeed to engrave the soil, to tear it. This image of the plow that digs and splits the earth is also found in most biblical uses. Biblical Hebrew thus expresses a well-known peasant reality: the brutal and regular work that sustains the Israelite.
H2758.emploi: The word charish appears only three times in the Hebrew Bible. In Genesis 45:6, Joseph announces seven years without plowing during the great famine — a situation of absolute catastrophe where life stops. In Exodus 34:21, at the heart of the Sabbath prescriptions, God prohibits plowing on the seventh day, even at peak agricultural activity — which shows that Sabbath rest takes precedence over any economic imperative. In 1 Samuel 8:12, Samuel warns Israel that the king will take his sons to plow his fields — this forced labor is a sign of royal oppression. The word thus marks critical moments when plowing becomes a matter of survival, justice, or religious obedience.
H2758.portee: This word reminds the reader that the work of the land is at the heart of human life according to the Bible — it is not a punishment, but a duty given from creation. But it also emphasizes that even this essential plowing must not divert the believer from resting and worshiping God: the Sabbath is inviolable. Finally, it denounces the abuse of power when a king diverts young men to cultivate his properties — plowing then becomes unjust servitude.

sens: Having a high temperature, burning
Causing a sensation of suffocation or physical discomfort
H2759.detail:
1. The word denotes the intense heat of the sun or wind. In Jonah 4:8, the hot east wind that blows on Jonah is so scorching that, combined with the sun beating down on his head, it causes him physical distress and leads him to wish for death.
2. Beyond simple temperature, "hot" evokes an overwhelming, suffocating heat that affects the entire body and makes existence intolerable. It is a hostile heat, causing suffering rather than comfort.
H2759.origine: The Hebrew word חֲרִישִׁי (charischi) likely comes from a root meaning "to burn" or "to be ardent." It is related to the idea of intense heat and destructive fervor. The context of the text speaks of a wind that comes to dry up and consume, evoking the biblical image of the desert where heat becomes a hostile force.
H2759.emploi: The word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Jonah 4:8. It describes the hot wind that God sends to increase Jonah's suffering. This hot wind adds to the heat of the rising sun to create a situation that becomes unbearable for the prophet. The usage is very localized and specific to this dramatic scene.
H2759.portee: This overwhelming heat reminds us that God can use natural elements to teach and transform his prophets. For Jonah, the brutal heat of the hot wind becomes a pedagogical instrument: it forces him to renounce his pride and accept God's compassion for Nineveh. The reader discovers how physical discomfort can become a school of wisdom.

sens: To cook meat exposed to fire or direct heat
To prepare food by transforming it through cooking
H2760.detail:
1. To roast means to cook meat by exposing it to fire or direct heat, making it edible and pleasant to the taste. It is cooking by fire, simpler than boiling: game is placed on coals or above the fire. In Proverbs 12:27, the slothful does not "roast" his game: he lacks the energy to complete this minimal task of meal preparation.
2. More broadly, roasting means to prepare, to transform a raw material by heat to derive benefit from it. This concrete image of cooking illustrates the theme of the verse: the active man transforms what he hunts into useful food, while the slothful lets his catch rot for lack of willingness to prepare it.
H2760.origine: The Hebrew verb חָרַךְ (charakh) denotes the action of cooking by direct heat. The first gloss "to set in motion" and the second "to roast" may seem distant, but they share the idea of active transformation: one moves the meat over the fire, putting it into action to cook it. The word belongs to the concrete vocabulary of cooking and daily Israeli life.
H2760.emploi: This verb appears only once in the Bible, in Proverbs 12:27. It is not found elsewhere, making it a rare word. The context of the verse is that of the parable of work and laziness: the slothful hunts game (minimum effort), but does not even prepare it to eat (absent effort). The verb "to roast" symbolizes here ordinary work, the logical and necessary follow-up to effort: having game is not enough, it must be cooked to be useful. The word is used in its literal and concrete sense, but in a wisdom text that uses the image to teach a moral lesson.
H2760.portee: This verse invites every believer not to stop at the beginning of a task, but to carry it through to completion with diligence. The slothful wastes his resources and opportunities; the active man transforms what he possesses into true wealth. It is an invitation to cultivate the habit of completed work and to see in every task, even humble, a responsibility before God.

sens: To partially consume by fire, to blacken the surface without destroying
To be damaged or scorched by heat
H2761.detail:
1. This verb describes the action of fire that blackens or slightly consumes the surface of something, without completely destroying it. It is less radical than "to reduce to ashes": it involves partial burning, scorching. In Daniel 3:27, after the three young men have been thrown into the blazing furnace, the text emphasizes that "the hair on their heads was not singed" — in other words, the extreme heat did not even scorch or damage their hair, making the miracle even more striking.
2. By extension, the word can refer to being damaged or marked by heat, whether it be hair, clothing, or skin. The absence of burns becomes proof that the fire had no power over these men.
H2761.origine: This Aramaic word is closely related to the Hebrew root חָרַר (charar, "to burn" or "to be burning"), which denotes the action of burning or consuming. The Hebrew verb originally evokes intense and destructive heat. The Aramaic takes up this image of fire and heat to describe what is scorched or damaged on the surface by contact with fire.
H2761.emploi: This Aramaic verb appears only once in the Bible, in Daniel 3:27. It arises in the account of the judgment of the three young Hebrews thrown into King Nebuchadnezzar's blazing furnace. The text lists everything the fire could not do: it did not burn their hair, did not damage their clothing, did not touch their skin. This rare verb thus emphasizes, by its very mention, the absence of the fire's effect — the miracle residing precisely in what the fire did not burn that it should normally consume or scorch.
H2761.portee: This word highlights divine faithfulness and protection. When the three young men refuse to worship the golden statue, God protects them in a tangible and verifiable way: no trace of fire on their bodies, not even a slight burn. For the reader, this affirms that trust in God during trial is not in vain — the real danger is neutralized, and God makes visible the signs of His intervention.

sens: Grill or open latticework
Opening through which one can look or see
H2762.detail:
1. A lattice is a grill or an interweaving of bars, slats, or wires — like an open fence or mesh — that allows light and sight to pass through without offering a direct view. In Song of Solomon 2:9, the beloved looks through the lattice, meaning through this partial grill, so that he is only partially seen.
2. It is also the opening itself — a window or bay — through which one can see outside or be seen from outside, but always in a veiled or filtered manner by the open structure. The lattice creates a relative intimacy: one sees each other, but not completely, hence the poetry of the scene — the beloved looking without being fully visible.
H2762.origine: The Hebrew word חֲרַכִּים (cherakkîm) comes from the root חרך, which evokes the idea of engraving, cutting, or piercing. The lattice is therefore etymologically what is "pierced" or "cut" to leave openings — a structure that alternates solids and voids. The open structure is the visible trace of this cutting action.
H2762.emploi: This word appears only once in the Bible, in Song of Solomon 2:9. It specifically designates the open lattice — probably a lattice window — through which the beloved looks at his friend. The poetic context emphasizes the intimacy tinged with mystery: there is a gentle barrier, a porous boundary that both separates and brings together the two lovers. It is a detail that enriches the image of longing and veiled presence.
H2762.portee: This lattice symbolizes the gentle limit between the two lovers — neither a total wall nor absolute transparency. For the reader, it reminds that love can exist through obstacles, and that waiting, looking from a distance, is itself beautiful and desirable. It is an image of sustained desire, of intimacy that crosses barriers without destroying them.

sens: To place something or someone under a ban, completely removing it from common use
To dedicate a person or thing to total destruction, exterminating it without mercy
To irrevocably consecrate to God as an offering or judgment
H2763A.detail:
1. In the laws of Israel, "vowed to destruction" means formally prohibiting the use of something or its preservation: it becomes subject to an absolute prohibition and can no longer be used by anyone. It is a serious legal and religious act that definitively separates the object from the ordinary world (Leviticus 27:28).
2. In war, this verb describes the total destruction of a conquered city or people: not only the combatants but also the women, children, livestock, and all property are systematically killed or burned. Joshua "devotes" Ai to destruction, meaning he completely annihilates it as a divine judgment, and this act is repeated for other cities (Joshua 6:21; Joshua 11:12).
3. The term also reveals a religious dimension: it is an offering of destruction made to the Lord, a way of acknowledging that victory comes from God and that all this people or these goods belong to Him forever, removed from the living world (Numbers 21:2-3).
H2763A.origine: The verb חָרַם (haram) comes from a root meaning "to cut off" or "to separate." The derived noun חֵרֶם (hérem) designates the ban itself, the thing or person subject to a sentence of annihilation. This practice of sacred prohibition was also known in ancient Near Eastern cultures, but it took on a theological significance in Israel: placing something "under the hérem" means placing it under the irrevocable judgment of the Lord.
H2763A.emploi: The verb appears 47 times in the Old Testament, primarily concentrated in the books of conquest (Joshua, Judges, 1 Samuel) and in accounts of holy war. It first describes the systematic killing of Canaanite peoples during the conquest: the laws of Deuteronomy command Israel to "devote to destruction" the idolatrous nations (Deuteronomy 7:2; Deuteronomy 20:17). The word is also used in contexts of violating this ban: when Saul refuses to devote King Agag and the best livestock, it is a serious breach of divine orders (1 Samuel 15:9). Later, the prophets use it to announce the Lord's judgment on Israel's enemies (Jeremiah 25:9; Isaiah 34:2).
H2763A.portee: This word confronts the reader with the reality of divine judgment in the history of Israel. It is not an arbitrary human cruelty, but a sentence pronounced by God against idolatry and evil, marking the absolute separation between the people of the Lord and the nations that reject Him. For the Christian, this ancient term reminds us that God takes rebellion and the refusal of His Word seriously, and invites reflection on the grace we have received in Jesus Christ, who saved us from this judgment.

sens: To have a flattened or squashed nose
To present a visible physical defect
H2763B.detail:
1. To have a flattened or squashed nose: the word describes a nose whose bridge is flattened or broken, giving the face a characteristic appearance. In Leviticus 21:18, this physical defect is listed among the infirmities that prohibited a man from serving as a priest in the temple.
2. To present a visible physical defect: more broadly, the word designates any bodily defect that renders it imperfect or incomplete. The law of sacrifices and priestly service enumerated these defects to remind that only what was whole and without blemish was worthy to be offered to God.
H2763B.origine: The Hebrew verb comes from a root meaning "to split," "to tear," or "to mutilate." The basic image is that of a part of the body torn, broken, or crushed. In this passage, it applies to a flattened nose, as if its bridge had been broken. The same root can designate other forms of mutilation or division.
H2763B.emploi: This verb appears only once in the Bible, in Leviticus 21:18. It is included in the list of bodily defects that rendered a priest unfit for service in the tabernacle. These defects — blindness, lameness, flat nose, overly long limb — illustrated the principle that the service of God required physical perfection, a symbol of purity and dignity. This principle reflected the holiness of the temple and the God being served there.
H2763B.portee: This requirement for physical perfection reminds us that the Mosaic law established standards of ritual purity. However, the Gospel reveals that God looks at the heart, not the appearance: Jesus welcomed and healed the infirm and the sick, showing that true dignity comes from faith, not from physical perfection. This contrast invites the Christian to place their trust in Christ rather than in their own righteousness or strength.

sens: Property or person consecrated to God and removed from ordinary use
What is vowed to total destruction without reprieve
Absolute prohibition against touching, taking, or using something
Capital penalty applied to anyone who transgresses this prohibition
H2764A.detail:
1. The devoted thing is primarily a sacred property, entirely reserved for God: it cannot be sold or redeemed, and it belongs forever to the sanctuary and its priests. In Leviticus 27:21, a field "devoted" at the jubilee becomes permanently the property of the priest, as it has been set apart from human domain.
2. In holy wars, this notion takes on a destructive dimension: Joshua 6:17 commands that Jericho be "devoted" to the Lord by a ban — the entire city must be annihilated, no mercy, no recovery of spoils is permitted. It is the execution of divine judgment.
3. To prohibit something is to place it under this curse: in Joshua 7:11, the Israelites have "taken devoted things," meaning they have stolen what was reserved for God alone and should not have been touched. Touching such a thing is to violate a sacred boundary.
4. Anyone who transgresses this prohibition deserves death: Joshua 7:15 states that the thief of devoted goods "shall be burned with fire, he and all that belongs to him." The violation of what is devoted to God calls for the total destruction of the guilty party and their household.
H2764A.origine: The Hebrew word חֵרֶם (chérem) comes from a root meaning "to separate" or "to cut off." It designates what is cut off from the ordinary world, placed under a sacred ban or a sentence of death. This idea is found in Aramaic and other Semitic languages: it is a very ancient religious term, expressing God's absolute power over life and death, and the necessity of total obedience to His commands.
H2764A.emploi: This word appears 22 times in the Old Testament, primarily in the books of the Law (Leviticus, Numbers, Deuteronomy) and in accounts of conquest (Joshua), as well as in other prophetic contexts. In Leviticus and Numbers, it concerns sacred goods or offerings removed from circulation. In Jericho (Joshua 6), the entire city is devoted to destruction — it is an act of holy war where God eliminates the enemy by this means. The incident of Achan (Joshua 7) shows the serious crime represented by the theft of devoted goods: his entire family pays the price. In 1 Kings 20:42, King Ahab spared a man whom God had "devoted" by a ban to death — this transgression will cost lives. The word thus expresses both sacred separation (in worship) and the sentence of destruction without appeal (in war and punishment).
H2764A.portee: This term reveals two essential realities: first, that certain things belong entirely to God and cannot be diverted for our purposes — it is a call to holiness and respect for the boundaries He establishes. Secondly, it shows that disobeying God's order exposes one to merciless judgment. For the Christian, this reminds us that our very lives are devoted to the Lord: we no longer belong to ourselves, and this "devotion" to God, far from being a loss, is our only true freedom.

sens: Fishing or hunting net, mesh fabric for capturing
Trap, bond that holds and imprisons
Destruction, capture of a nation or people
H2764B.detail:
1. The net is a fishing or hunting equipment: a woven mesh fabric that is thrown into the water or over an animal to capture it. Ezekiel 47:10 describes fishermen spreading nets from En-Gedi to En-Eglaim, a concrete image of daily work.

2. The net becomes an image of the trap and imprisonment. Ecclesiastes 7:26 compares the heart of a wicked woman to a net where the sinner gets caught, while the one who pleases God escapes: the net holds the one who jumps in without vigilance.

3. In the prophecies of Ezekiel and Habakkuk, God's net symbolizes His military capture or judgment upon the nations. Ezekiel 32:3 announces that God will spread His net over Pharaoh among a multitude of peoples, and Habakkuk 1:15 shows the net of the conqueror drawing all peoples to him: inevitable and organized destruction.
H2764B.origine: The Hebrew word חֵרֶם (chérem) comes from a root evoking the idea of digging, piercing, hence the initial image of the perforated, meshed fabric. The word belongs to the family of nets and capture devices. This vocabulary of net expresses both the technique of capture and the vulnerability of the prey.
H2764B.emploi: The word appears 9 times, mostly in the prophets Ezekiel (4 times) and Habakkuk (3 times). In Ezekiel, the net first describes the work of fishermen (47:10), then becomes the image of divine judgment upon the nations (26:5, 26:14, 32:3). In Habakkuk, the conqueror spreads his net to capture the peoples (1:15 to 1:17). In Ecclesiastes 7:26, it is the moral trap where the wicked woman catches the sinner. The word remains concrete in its image but symbolically charged: from simple fishing equipment to God's sovereign judgment.
H2764B.portee: This word reminds us that sin is a trap where one gradually gets caught, and that God controls all events—even those that seem threatening—within the net of His justice. It invites the reader to moral vigilance and trust in divine sovereignty.

sens: Fortified city in the territory of Naphtali
H2765.detail: Horem is a fortified city that belonged to the territory assigned to the tribe of Naphtali during the division of the promised land. It is mentioned in Joshua 19:38 among the nineteen cities of the lot of Naphtali, alongside Jireon, Migdal-El, Beth-Anath, and Beth-Shemesh.
H2765.origine: The name means "sacred" in Hebrew, probably because this place was consecrated or held religious significance for the tribe. Like many biblical cities, the name reflects either a characteristic of the site or its particular status.
H2765.emploi: Horem is mentioned only once in the Bible, in Joshua 19:38, during the enumeration of the fortified cities assigned to Naphtali. This list is part of the account of the distribution of the promised land among the twelve tribes of Israel after the conquest.

sens: Priest of the house of David responsible for the Temple service
Family of priests and Levites who returned from exile
Descendants of the exiles who returned with Zerubbabel
H2766G.detail:
1. Harim is first a priest during the time of King David, responsible for the third rotation of the Temple service (1 Chronicles 24:8). As the priestly service was divided into courses that took turns, Harim represents one of these teams of priests.

2. Harim then refers to a family of exiled priests who returned from Babylon with Zerubbabel: one thousand seventeen members of this house resumed their place in Israel (Ezra 2:39 and Nehemiah 7:42). The large number shows the importance of this lineage.

3. Finally, the name Harim is associated with several individuals from this family who participated in the religious reform during Nehemiah's time, notably by repudiating foreign wives (Ezra 10:21 and 10:31), confirming that this family held a role of religious and civil responsibility in the reconstruction.
H2766G.origine: The name Harim comes from the Hebrew root "herem" which means "to consecrate," "to dedicate to God." This name thus expresses the idea of a person or lineage set apart for divine service. It is a significant name for a priestly family, as the priests themselves were consecrated to the service of the Temple.
H2766G.emploi: Harim appears five times in the biblical texts, always in the historical books (1 Chronicles, Ezra, Nehemiah). The name first designates an individual priest from David's time (1 Chronicles 24:8), then transforms into a dynastic family name. This family survives the Babylonian exile and returns in large numbers with Zerubbabel around 538 B.C. The descendants of Harim play an active role in the religious and civil reorganization of Israel after the exile, notably by accepting the reforms of Governor Nehemiah.
H2766G.portee: The case of Harim illustrates how God preserves and restores those who are dedicated to Him.
