Despite exile and deportation, this priestly family returns in strength, maintaining its religious identity and authority. It is an encouraging testimony: those who are "dedicated" to God are never completely abandoned, even in the midst of captivity.

sens: Man of the Exile and Return period
Family head of those returning from exile
H2766H.detail: Harim is a name borne by several important men at the time when the Jews returned from captivity in Babylon. In the lists of the Return, it notably designates the head of a family whose sons, numbering three hundred twenty, ascend to Jerusalem with Zerubbabel (Ezra 2:32; Nehemiah 7:35). His name means "consecrated" or "dedicated"—an image of one who belongs to God and His restoration project.
H2766H.origine: The name Harim comes from the Hebrew root meaning "to consecrate," "to vow," or "to set apart." It evokes the idea of something or someone reserved for God, separated for sacred use. It is a theophoric name, carrying within it the relationship with the divine.
H2766H.emploi: Harim appears twice in the preserved biblical texts: in the catalog of families returning from Babylonian exile, recorded in Ezra 2:32, and in a parallel version in Nehemiah 7:35. In these two passages, Harim is presented as the family head whose descendants count three hundred twenty souls. These lists of the Return show that Harim was a significant figure in the community of exiles, influential enough for his entire lineage to be mentioned by name.

sens: Man of the Exile and Return period
Priest during the time of David
Family head of exiles returning with Zerubbabel
Magistrate under Nehemiah
H2766I.detail: 1. Harim is a man mentioned only once in the Bible, at the time when Nehemiah restores the walls of Jerusalem: he is the father of Malchijah, who participates in this reconstruction (Nehemiah 3:11). 2. The name Harim also designates a priest during the time of King David, responsible for the third service of worship at the temple. 3. A Harim is the head of an important family of exiles: 1017 people from his house return from captivity in Babylon with Zerubbabel to rebuild the temple. 4. Another Harim leads a smaller family: 320 people return with Zerubbabel. 5. A Harim also serves as a magistrate among the people under Nehemiah's authority during the reconstruction of Jerusalem.
H2766I.origine: The name Harim means "dedicated" or "consecrated." Several men bear this name in the Old Testament, reflecting its importance among the priestly and noble families of Israel, particularly after the return from the Babylonian exile.
H2766I.emploi: The only direct use of this name in the Bible is found in Nehemiah 3:11, where Harim is identified as the father of Malchijah, one of the overseers of the reconstruction of the walls of Jerusalem. However, Jewish traditions and biblical lists mention several characters bearing this name: priests from the time of David, heads of families of exiles returning from Babylon (with remarkably large numbers: over 1000 people for one of the families), and magistrates under Nehemiah. This name thus appears as that of an influential priestly lineage in Israel.

sens: man who signed the covenant under Nehemiah
H2766J.detail: Harim is a character mentioned only once in the Bible, in Nehemiah 10:27, where he is listed among those who affixed their seal to the covenant document made by the people who returned from Babylonian exile. He is one of the leaders or religious officials who solemnly committed to observing the Law of Moses and the decrees of the restored temple.
H2766J.origine: The name Harim means "dedicated" or "consecrated" in Hebrew, evoking a separation or sacred setting apart. Several namesakes bear this name in the history of Israel: a priest during the time of David, leaders of families of exiles who returned with Zerubbabel, and a priest during the time of Nehemiah. The one mentioned here belongs to the generation that rebuilt the temple and reorganized the community after the exile.
H2766J.emploi: Harim is named only once in the Bible, in Nehemiah 10:27, in the context of the restoration of Jerusalem after the Babylonian exile. He is among the signatories of the solemn covenant that the leaders, Levites, and priests of Judah made to commit to observing the Law. His name appears in a list of dignitaries who affixed their seal to this document of community commitment.
H2766J.portee: This passage shows that the reconstruction of Israel after the exile was not the work of a single leader, but a collective covenant made by many religious and civil leaders. Harim's role reminds us that faithfulness to God requires both personal and communal commitment, sealed by a solemn act. It illustrates how the restoration of worship and God's order comes through common decisions and solemn promises.

sens: priest and family leader during the Exile and return
signatory of the renewed covenant during Nehemiah's time
H2766K.detail:
1. Harim is a name borne by several important figures during the return from Babylonian exile. The most well-known is a family leader whose 1,017 members returned with Zerubbabel to rebuild the temple and Jerusalem. He represents one of the great families that participated in the restoration of the Jewish community after the captivity (Ezra 2:2).
2. In the time of Nehemiah, a Harim is among the signatories of the solemn covenant renewed by the people, alongside Meremoth and other leaders (Nehemiah 10:5). His name also appears in the list of priests of Jerusalem (Nehemiah 12:15), where he replaces Adna in the succession of priestly family leaders, showing his continuity of role in religious leadership.
H2766K.origine: The name Harim means "dedicated" or "consecrated." It derives from a root that evokes the idea of holy separation, set apart for God. This name reflects the commitment of this family to the Lord and the communal religious life.
H2766K.emploi: Harim primarily appears in the books of Ezra and Nehemiah, which recount the return from exile and the restoration of Jerusalem. The name first designates a family leader whose descendants were among the largest to return from Babylon, and then the priest who signs the renewed covenant at the time of Nehemiah (around 445 B.C.). It is an example of the religious and civil leaders who ensured the continuity of worship and the Jewish community after the desolation of the kingdom.

sens: City in southern Canaan conquered by Israel
H2767.detail: Horma is a city located in the southern part of ancient Canaan. It was initially inhabited by the Canaanites but was conquered by Israel and attached to the territory of Judah. Its name means "devotion" or "destruction," referring to how it was taken: the Israelites devoted it to the Lord by a ban, meaning they completely destroyed it as an offering to God (Numbers 21:3). The city appears in the lists of conquests by Joshua and in the boundaries of the territory of Judah (Joshua 15:30 and 19:4). It is also mentioned during the pursuit of the Israelites by the Amorites after their refusal to enter Canaan (Deuteronomy 1:44), and later in the history of David (1 Samuel 30:30).
H2767.origine: The Hebrew name חׇרְמָה (chor.mah) comes from the root חרם (chor), which means "to devote to destruction" or "to place under a ban." In biblical thought, "devoting by a ban" (Hebrew: חֵרֶם, chérem) meant dedicating something or someone to God irrevocably, often by destroying it. The name of this city thus commemorates this act of devotion: it was conquered and consecrated to the Lord in this way. It is also another name for Zephath (צְפַ֑ת), a Canaanite city.
H2767.emploi: Horma appears nine times in the Hebrew Bible. It is first mentioned in Numbers 14:45 and Numbers 21:3 in the account of its conquest by Israel — the Israelites devote it to the Lord by a ban and give it this name. It later appears in the account of Joshua's wars (Joshua 12:14) and in the lists of cities assigned to Judah (Joshua 15:30 and 19:4). Later, it is mentioned during the flight of the Israelites defeated by the Amorites (Deuteronomy 1:44) and in later passages (Judges 1:17, 1 Samuel 30:30, 1 Chronicles 4:30). Its appearance in these various contexts shows that it was a fortified city in southern Judah, strategically important in the history of Israel.

sens: Major mountain in the Middle East, northeastern border of Palestine
Boundary line between the territory of Israel and neighboring regions
Spectacular summit known for its beauty and majesty
H2768.detail: 1. Hermon is a high mountain that marks the northeastern boundary of the territory of Israel, between Palestine and Lebanon. It dominates the region and serves as a geographical landmark in descriptions of conquests (Deuteronomy 3:8: the conquered territory extends "to the mountain of Hermon"). 2. It delineates the borders of the land, notably the eastern territory that returned to the tribes after crossing the Jordan. Joshua 13:11 lists "all the mountain of Hermon" among the lands distributed. 3. It is a remarkable mountain, often associated with divine splendor: Psalm 89:13 mentions it alongside Tabor as a testament to God's creative power.
H2768.origine: The name Hermon means "sanctuary" or "sacred place" in Hebrew. The mountain, with its snow-capped peaks visible from afar, embodied in antiquity a place from which a transcendent presence emanates. Ancient peoples saw in high mountain sites spaces close to the divine.
H2768.emploi: Hermon appears thirteen times in Scripture, primarily in geographical descriptions related to the conquest and division of territory (Deuteronomy, Joshua, Chronicles). It delineates the domain of Og of Bashan and the lands granted to the northeastern tribes. The psalmists use it to evoke God's creative majesty and the splendor of His work (Psalm 133:3 mentions it in a poem about blessing and harmony).
H2768.portee: Hermon reminds us that God assigns boundaries and gives an inheritance to His people. This visible and unchanging mountain symbolizes God's faithfulness to His promises of land. It also invites the reader to contemplate the greatness of divine creation.

sens: Mountain massif with three peaks located at the northern border of Palestine and Lebanon
H2769.detail: 1. Hermon is the name of a great mountain that marks the northern boundary of the Promised Land. It stands at the border between Palestine and Lebanon, with three distinct peaks. It is a major mountain in the biblical landscape, covered with snow for much of the year. The psalmist, exiled far from Jerusalem, thinks of God from the land of Jordan, mentioning Hermon as a geographical landmark in the north of the promised land (Psalms 42:7).
H2769.origine: The Hebrew name hermon (חֶרְמוֹן) is related to the root הרם which means "to be high" or "elevated." Hermon literally means "the High Mountain" or "the Sacred Mountain," which suits this majestic mountain that dominates the landscape of Canaan. The term chermonim in the plural emphasizes its three distinct peaks.
H2769.emploi: The word appears only once in the Segond 1910 in this passage from Psalms. Hermon is mentioned as an important landmark of the biblical territory, particularly in descriptions of the northern Promised Land. It is also mentioned under its simple name (without the plural) in other passages of Scripture as a major geographical marker.
H2769.portee: Hermon reminds the believer of the vastness and majesty of God's creation. This high mountain, visible from afar, illustrates how the psalmist, physically distant from the temple in Jerusalem, remains connected to his God by contemplating His works. It is an invitation to recognize the divine presence even in the great spaces of nature.

sens: Curved tool with a sharp blade used for harvesting grains
Harvesting instrument that marks the beginning and end of field work
H2770.detail:
1. The sickle is a harvesting tool made up of a curved, sharp blade attached to a handle, which the reaper uses to cut ripe grains. In Deuteronomy 16:9, it is the moment when "the sickle is put into the grain" that signals the beginning of the Feast of Weeks: as soon as the harvest begins, seven weeks are counted until Pentecost.
2. This tool holds legal and social significance in the law of Israel. Deuteronomy 23:25 prohibits it: one cannot pass the sickle over another's field, even if one has the right to glean ears by hand. The distinction marks the difference between a modest personal harvest and a harvest that belongs to the owner of the field.
H2770.origine: The Hebrew word חֶרְמֵשׁ (chermesh) literally refers to the curved instrument used for harvesting. It is linked to the idea of "cutting" or "removing." This tool is attested in ancient Egypt and the Near East: it is a fundamental utensil of Mediterranean and Near Eastern agricultural life since ancient times.
H2770.emploi: The word appears twice in the Old Testament, only in Deuteronomy. It occurs in agricultural contexts related to the harvesting of grains and the civil laws of God's people. In Deuteronomy 16:9, the sickle marks the precise moment that triggers an important liturgical cycle. In Deuteronomy 23:25, it delineates what is permitted and what is forbidden during the harvest: one may glean by hand, but not harvest with the tool. These two uses show the importance of the sickle as a symbol and as a legal instrument.
H2770.portee: For God's people, the sickle reminds that the harvest belongs to the one who has sown and worked. It also marks the sacred moments of the liturgical calendar, linking field work to religious life. This law regarding the sickle taught Israel respect for property and justice toward one's neighbor, even in times of need.

sens: City in Mesopotamia where Abraham stopped before going to Canaan
Place of residence for Abraham's family after leaving Ur
Starting point for Abraham's journey to the promised land
H2771A.detail: 1. Charan is a city located in Mesopotamia, in the region of Padan-aram, between the Khabour and Euphrates rivers. It is where Abraham and his family settled after leaving Ur of the Chaldeans (Genesis 11:31), and where Abraham's father, Terach, died (Genesis 11:32). 2. The city was also the residence of Laban, Isaac's brother, and it is to Charan that Jacob fled to escape Esau's anger (Genesis 27:43; 28:10). It was on the way to Charan that Jacob had his vision of the ladder (Genesis 28:12). 3. From Charan, Abraham eventually left his family to embark on the journey to Canaan, the land that God had promised him (Genesis 12:4-5).
H2771A.origine: The name Charan means "mountaineer" or "one of the mountain," likely referring to the geography of the region. The city was an important center of the ancient Near East, a commercial crossroads in Mesopotamia. It also appears in Assyrian inscriptions under similar forms. The Septuagint, the Greek translation of the Old Testament, transcribes this name as Χαρράν (Charran).
H2771A.emploi: Charan appears ten times in the Hebrew and Greek Bible, mostly in the book of Genesis. It is the place where Abraham and his family stop after leaving Ur (Genesis 11:31-32), the anchor point of the patriarch's first period of travel. From Charan, Abraham ultimately departs alone for Canaan at the age of seventy-five, leaving his father Terach who dies there (Genesis 12:4-5). Later, Charan becomes significant again when Jacob, fleeing Esau, goes there to seek refuge with his uncle Laban (Genesis 27:43; 28:10). The name also appears in later historical contexts as a place of destination or trade (2 Kings 19:12; Ezekiel 27:23).
H2771A.portee: Charan marks a decisive step in the history of salvation: it is the breaking point where Abraham accepts to leave his family and security to follow God's call. The city itself is not a place of promise but a stage of separation and transition. It reminds that faith requires the believer to renounce not only material comfort but also family ties, to embark on the path that God indicates.

sens: Man of the tribe of Judah, son of Caleb
H2771B.detail: Haran is a minor character in the Old Testament, mentioned only once in the genealogy of the tribe of Judah. He is the son of Caleb and his concubine Ephah, and appears in the list of his descendants (1 Chronicles 2:46). The text informs us that he had a son named Gazez, thus continuing Caleb's lineage.
H2771B.origine: The name Haran means "mountaineer" or "one of the mountains," evoking the image of a person living in mountainous regions. This name was borne by several individuals in biblical history, including Abraham's brother, but this one refers to a simple descendant of Caleb, with no further details given about his life or actions in the Bible.
H2771B.emploi: Haran appears only once in the provided usages, in 1 Chronicles 2:46, where he is mentioned in Caleb's genealogy. He is presented as the son of Ephah and the father of Gazez, indicating his role as a link in the genealogical chain of the tribe of Judah. No other deeds or characteristics are reported about him.

sens: Inhabitant or native of Horonaim, a city in Moab
Specifically refers to Sanballat, an adversary of Nehemiah
H2772.detail:
1. An Horonite is someone from Horonaim, a city located in Moab, a region east of the Jordan. The term denotes the geographical and ethnic origin of a person, similar to saying "Parisian" or "Egyptian."
2. In the book of Nehemiah, this word specifically qualifies Sanballat, a character who strongly opposes the rebuilding of the wall of Jerusalem. When Sanballat learns of Nehemiah's arrival, he "was very displeased" (Nehemiah 2:10), and later he openly mocks the project with his allies (Nehemiah 2:19).
H2772.origine: The word comes from the name of the city of Horonaim in Moab. The Hebrew suffix "-i" (ִי) is used to form demonyms, that is, names designating a person's origin or belonging to a place or group. It is the same process that creates "Egyptian" from the name "Egypt" or "Benjaminite" from "Benjamin."
H2772.emploi: The word appears only three times in the Bible, exclusively in Nehemiah, always referring to Sanballat. He is a political and religious adversary who opposes Nehemiah's project to rebuild the walls of Jerusalem. He first appears in 2:10 where he is informed of Nehemiah's arrival and reacts with hostility, then in 2:19 where he joins others to ridicule and threaten the builders, and finally in 13:28 where he is mentioned as a relative by marriage of a priestly family. His status as a foreigner (Horonite) perhaps underscores Moab's opposition to the Jewish project.
H2772.portee: This word shows how the Bible precisely names the adversaries of God and His people. Sanballat embodies human resistance to God's plans, and his title of "Horonite" positions him as a stranger to the people of God. For the reader, it serves as a reminder that even external obstacles and mockery from enemies do not prevent God from accomplishing His work of restoration.

sens: City of Moab
Place of refuge and escape during disasters
H2773.detail:
1. Choronaim is a city located in Moab, a region east of Jordan. It appears in prophetic passages that describe the misfortunes of Moab.
2. The city is mentioned as a place where cries of distress and weeping resound during invasions and ravages of Moab (Jeremiah 48:3, 48:5). It marks an important geographical boundary: "From Zoar to Choronaim" (Jeremiah 48:34) indicates the extent of the disaster affecting the entire territory.
H2773.origine: The name literally means "two caves" in Hebrew. This etymology likely evokes the topography of the region, perhaps marked by caves or geological formations. The city thus derives its name from visible natural features of the Moabite landscape.
H2773.emploi: Choronaim appears in five biblical passages, primarily in the prophecies of Isaiah and Jeremiah concerning the judgment of Moab. In Isaiah 15:5, it is mentioned alongside other Moabite cities (Zoar, Eglath-Shelishiyah) as a destination of escape during a devastation. In the three passages of Jeremiah 48 (verses 3, 5, and 34), Choronaim is a geographical landmark where the lamentations and cries of a distressed population resonate. The city symbolizes the extent of divine judgment over the entire Moabite territory.
H2773.portee: Choronaim reminds the reader that God's judgment on the nations extends to all places, from the largest to the smallest, and that no geographical refuge escapes His justice. This small city, though distant and little known, is worthy of being named by the prophets because it is part of the people of God to whom He speaks.

sens: Man of the tribe of Asher during the divided monarchy
H2774.detail: Harnépher is a man of the tribe of Asher, mentioned only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 7:36. He is the son of Tzophach and brother to several other men of his tribe: Suach, Shual, Beri, Jimra, Bezer, Hod, Shammah, Shilscha, Ithran, and Beera. His name literally means "one who pants" or "one who breathes with effort," which may evoke breathlessness or ardor. No details are given about his deeds or life; he appears in the genealogies merely as a link in a long chain of descendants of Asher.
H2774.origine: The name Harnépher comes from the Hebrew root "harnaph" (חרנף), which means "to pant" or "to breathe with difficulty." This root evokes physical effort, labored breathing. It belongs to a family of words describing states of movement or tension. The name thus reflects a quality or characteristic related to effort or ardor, common in Hebrew onomastics where personal names often incorporate images drawn from nature or human behavior.
H2774.emploi: Harnépher appears only once in the entire Bible, in 1 Chronicles 7:36. This passage lists the descendants of Asher during the divided monarchy, grouped in genealogies. His name is simply cited in the list of the sons of Tzophach, without mention of his own children or particular deeds. This brief appearance places him among those many biblical figures whose names and places in the genealogy are retained in the Bible, as a witness to God's faithfulness to the twelve tribes of Israel.

sens: luminous celestial body that lights the day
moment of sunset, end of the day
power or force that cannot be stopped
H2775A.detail:
1. The sun is the celestial body that shines during the day and brings light to the earth. It is the most powerful visible object in the sky, regulating the rhythm of life (Judges 14:18 speaks of sunset as a temporal landmark).
2. Sunset marks the end of the day and the transition to night. In the passage from Judges 14:18, the people of the city speak on the seventh day "before sunset," showing that this moment is well identified as a natural and important boundary.
3. The sun can symbolize an invincible or unavoidable power. In Job 9:7, God "commands the sun, and it does not shine": this image expresses that only God can dominate what seems the most powerful and constant in creation.
H2775A.origine: The Hebrew word cheresh comes from an ancient root designating the solar body. It is simply formed to directly name this visible celestial object par excellence. The word is infrequent in the Hebrew Bible, suggesting that other more common terms (like chamash) were preferred to speak of the sun in everyday language.
H2775A.emploi: The word cheresh appears twice in the Hebrew Bible. It first denotes a temporal landmark (Judges 14:18, where sunset marks the end of the seventh day) and a cosmic reality over which only God has absolute authority (Job 9:7, where the sun becomes the image of what seems immutable but which God can stop). These two contexts show that the sun is viewed as a visible, measurable reality subject to divine will.
H2775A.portee: The sun reminds us that everything that seems stable, powerful, or inevitable remains under God's control. Even the celestial body that governs day and night can be halted by the Creator. This truth encourages the believer to recognize that God is above all creation and all natural forces.

sens: Contagious skin disease characterized by intense itching and lesions
Skin condition that adds to the wounds and diseases sent by God as punishment
H2775B.detail:
1. The teigne is a very unpleasant skin disease that causes itching and rashes. It is a contagious condition that is well known in hot and humid regions like ancient Egypt. In Deuteronomy 28:27, it is listed among the plagues sent by God: "The Lord will strike you with the boils of Egypt, with hemorrhoids, with scab, and with teigne, from which you cannot be healed."
2. In this biblical context, the teigne is not simply an ordinary disease: it represents a form of divine punishment, associated with other plagues. The text suggests that this disease is incurable, reinforcing the idea that it is sent as a consequence of unfaithfulness to the covenant.
H2775B.origine: The Hebrew word חֶרֶס (cherès) refers to a pruritic skin condition, likely related to a root evoking itching or irritation. This term specific to Deuteronomy translates a well-known medical reality of the ancient world: skin diseases caused by humidity and hot climate. The word reflects the concrete observation of the ailments that affected ancient populations.
H2775B.emploi: The word appears only once in the Bible, in Deuteronomy 28:27, in the series of curses that the Lord promises to send upon the people who transgress His covenant. The teigne appears alongside other plagues: the boils of Egypt, hemorrhoids, and scab. This enumeration shows that God would strike the unfaithful people with multiple and incurable dermatological diseases. The context is that of the blessings and curses of Deuteronomy, where the consequences of obedience or disobedience are described in their most raw details.
H2775B.portee: This mention reminds the reader that God's curses are not abstract: they affect the body and cause real and lasting suffering. The incurable teigne symbolizes a punishment from which one cannot escape by one's own strength. For the believer, this passage invites a serious consideration of the covenant with God and the grave consequences of unfaithfulness, while understanding that no disease, even incurable according to men, escapes divine power.

sens: Mountain of Moab where the Amorites lived
H2776G.detail: Hérès is a mountain located in Moab, the region east of the Jordan. It is where Gideon pursued the Midianites and halted his pursuit (Judges 8:13). The name means "the sun" in Hebrew, perhaps because this mountain faced south or was visible from afar under the sun.
H2776G.origine: The Hebrew word חֶרֶס (Hérès) literally means "the sun." It is a place name that plays on this image of the sun, likely due to its geographical position or striking appearance. The proper name is formed from this common root in Hebrew and Aramaic.
H2776G.emploi: Hérès appears only once in the Bible, in Judges 8:13. It is the point where Gideon returns from his pursuit of the Midianites after his victory with his three hundred men. The context of this verse shows that it was a well-known location at the time, serving as a geographical landmark marking the end of Gideon's military expedition.

sens: Mountain of Canaan
Place of Amorite dominance
Border region of Joseph's territory
H2776H.detail:
1. Har-Hérès is a mountain in Canaan, whose name literally means "mountain of the sun" (har = mountain, hérès = sun). It is a mountainous region that marks an important geographical location in the early conquest of Canaan.
2. It is a place inhabited by the Amorites who resisted Israel's settlement. During the allocation of territories, the tribe of Joseph was initially unable to drive them out completely, as reported in Judges 1:35.
3. Gradually, however, the people of Israel imposed their authority: the Amorites were reduced to subjugation and forced to pay tribute, thus marking the consolidation of Israelite power in this region.
H2776H.origine: The name Har-Hérès literally means "mountain of the sun." Hérès comes from the same root as the word for sun in Hebrew. This same location is also known by another name: Beth-shemesh, which means "house of the sun" — both names refer to the same geographical and religious reality of the sun as a landmark in the landscape.
H2776H.emploi: Har-Hérès appears only once in the Bible, in Judges 1:35. This passage describes the initial phase of the conquest of Canaan, when the tribes of Israel were settling in the land and gradually reducing the resistance of the indigenous populations. This mountain is mentioned alongside Ajalon and Shaalbim as a center of Amorite resistance, located in the territory that would belong to the house of Joseph (Ephraim and Manasseh). The context shows the transition from initial failure to gradual success: at first, the Israelites could not drive them out; then, through persistence and strength, they subdued them.
H2776H.portee: This account in Judges 1:35 reminds the reader that God's promise regarding the land was realized gradually, not through a single overwhelming victory, but through persistent occupation and consolidation of power. This encourages the believer to persevere in fulfilling divine promises, even when initial obstacles seem insurmountable.

sens: shard or fragment of broken pottery
gate or entrance named after a place where pottery was worked or sold
H2777.detail: 1. The word primarily refers to a piece of broken pottery or ceramic — the concrete image is that of shards, fragments of broken vessels found throughout ancient cities. 2. In Jeremiah 19:2, the "pottery gate" was likely a gate in Jerusalem named so because it was a potters' quarter, a place where terracotta objects were made and sold. The Hebrews often named city gates after the trades or places found there.
H2777.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root meaning "to dig" or "to scrape" — for making pottery involves shaping clay by digging and molding it. The same family of words in Hebrew evokes clay, the potter's work, and terracotta objects.
H2777.emploi: This word appears only once in the Bible, in Jeremiah 19:2. Jeremiah is to go to the pottery gate to pronounce an oracle of disaster against Judah. This context reveals that this gate was a real geographical location in Jerusalem, a passage to the valley of Ben-Hinnom. The prophet proclaims there that God will make the disobedient people like broken fragments, as broken pottery — the word "pottery" thus resonates with the judgment that Jeremiah announces.
H2777.portee: This passage shows that God sends His prophet to announce judgment in the ordinary places of the city, where simple people live and work. The metaphor of broken pottery reminds us that sin breaks humanity like a fragile vessel, but it also invites repentance, for a potter can remake a destroyed vessel.

sens: Address someone with contemptuous words, to cover them with shame
To challenge someone, to defy their authority
To offend God, to blaspheme Him through acts or words
To despise, to belittle someone
H2778A.detail:
1. To insult someone means to say mean and humiliating words that cover them with shame. David responds to the giant Goliath who has provoked him: "You come against me with a sword... but I come against you in the name of the Lord Almighty, the God of the armies of Israel, whom you have insulted" (1 Samuel 17:45). The enemy has spoken words of contempt against the people of Israel and their God.
2. To challenge someone means to defy them, to refuse to respect them and show that one does not fear them. In Gideon's battle, the enemies "faced" death (Judges 5:18) — they ran bravely towards it, without fear. This is also why Goliath "challenged" the Israelites day after day.
3. To insult God means to blaspheme Him, to treat Him with disrespect through one's acts or words. The king of Assyria "insulted the Lord" by saying that no god could defeat him: he threatened God as an enemy (2 Kings 19:23).
4. This verb can also mean to despise someone, to belittle them, particularly the weak or the poor. To insult the poor is to cover them with shame and contempt.
H2778A.origine: This root evokes the idea of wounding through words, of covering with shame. It refers to a verbal attack intended to humiliate or challenge. In the Hebrew Bible, this verb belongs to the vocabulary of shame and honor, two fundamental values of Semitic culture. An insult is not just a vain word: it wounds honor and reputation.
H2778A.emploi: This verb appears 38 times in biblical Hebrew, mainly in the Psalms, historical books, and among the prophets. It describes situations where someone is covered with shame by words or acts of contempt. Goliath "challenges" Israel in insult (1 Samuel 17). The psalmists complain about enemies who insult them (Psalms 44:17, 79:12). The king of Assyria insults the Lord by boasting that he can defeat His people (2 Kings 19:23). The verb also applies to insults directed at the poor (Proverbs 14:31, 17:5). Each time, it involves a word or attitude that belittles, challenges, or wounds.
H2778A.portee: This word reminds us that words carry serious weight: to insult someone is to attack their honor and dignity. To insult God is an act of rebellion that denies and provokes Him. For the Christian, this verb invites one to watch their words, not to cover with shame those who are weak or poor, and to recognize that God does not tolerate insults without consequence.

sens: To stay somewhere during the cold season
To remain and maintain oneself in a place through the winter months
H2778B.detail: 1. The verb חָרַף refers to the action of spending the winter in a place, meaning to stay there and survive during the cold season. In Isaiah 18:6, the beasts of the earth "will spend the winter" on the abandoned corpses: this is an image of permanence and occupation of the land. 2. The word more broadly evokes the idea of dwelling, of remaining established somewhere for an extended period, during which life is tested by cold and difficulty. It is an image of persistent presence and survival.
H2778B.origine: The root חָרַף belongs to the family of Hebrew verbs related to climate and seasons. It is associated with the image of the harshness of winter, the cold that forces one to stay and establish oneself. The verb concretely refers to the experience of enduring the difficult months of winter in a given place.
H2778B.emploi: The word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Isaiah 18:6. It is used concerning wild beasts that occupy the corpses of God's enemies throughout the winter: an image of desolation and complete abandonment. Its meaning is clearly that of "to stay, to dwell during the winter." The prophetic context emphasizes the idea of a lasting and humiliating occupation.
H2778B.portee: This word reminds us that the Scriptures use concrete images — seasons, climate, physical presence — to speak of God's judgment and its consequences. It invites us to meditate on the reality of punishments and the seriousness of the abandonment of the wicked.

sens: Woman promised or destined to a man by an engagement
H2778C.detail: 1. The word describes a woman who has been promised or destined to a man through a contract or engagement. In Leviticus 19:20, it refers to a slave woman "betrothed" to another man: she already belongs to someone else through this engagement, even if she has not yet married that man.
H2778C.origine: The Hebrew root fundamentally means "to acquire" or "to obtain." The meaning of "fiancée" comes from the idea that through betrothal, a woman is "acquired" or destined for a man: an engagement creates a bond of ownership or reservation. It is a legal and social image: the betrothed woman is "assigned" to her future husband before the marriage itself.
H2778C.emploi: The word appears only once in the Bible, in Leviticus 19:20. It designates a slave who has been promised to another man. The legal context shows that this engagement creates an obligation: a third party who would have relations with this woman commits a transgression, although the punishment is less severe than that of complete adultery, since she does not have the status of a free married woman (she is not "freed").
H2778C.portee: This verse reminds us that in the Law of Moses, engagements and promises (including betrothals) have legal and moral significance. It also shows how God protected the most vulnerable, even slaves, by recognizing the validity of their commitments.

sens: cold season of the year, between autumn and spring
cold, frost
winter house (heated dwelling for the cold season)
absence of warmth or spiritual life
H2779.detail: 1. Winter is the cold season that regularly returns: in Genesis 8:22, after the Flood, God promises that "cold and heat, summer and winter will never cease" — it is the natural order of things that repeats. 2. The cold is what characterizes winter and makes work difficult: in Proverbs 20:4, the lazy man refuses to plow because of the cold, and later he regrets having nothing to harvest. 3. Winter houses are specially designed dwellings for the cold season, with a fire for warmth: in Jeremiah 36:22, the king sits in his winter house with a fire in front of him, and Amos 3:15 speaks of winter houses and summer houses, showing that the wealthy had multiple dwellings according to the seasons. 4. Winter can also evoke what is dead, frozen, or abandoned: in a spiritual context, it is the image of a lack of warmth and life.
H2779.origine: The Hebrew word חֹרֶף comes from a root that evokes cold and cooling. In ancient Hebrew, it primarily designates the cold season and the months that accompany it. The word is linked to the idea of a decrease in heat and light, phenomena visible in the Mediterranean and Palestinian climate where winters can be harsh.
H2779.emploi: This word appears 7 times in the Hebrew Bible, almost exclusively in wisdom literature (books of wisdom) and the prophets. In Genesis 8:22, it refers to winter as part of the created order that God established forever. In Psalms 74:17, it is associated with summer as an element of creation fixed by God. In Proverbs 20:4, it takes on a moral significance: the cold of winter becomes the excuse of the lazy man who refuses to work. In Jeremiah 36:22 and Amos 3:15, the word designates the winter houses of kings and the great, revealing the luxury and wealth of the powerful. Job 29:4 is the only usage where it seems to have a different meaning ("to watch"), probably with a nuance of benevolent protection.
H2779.portee: For the Christian reader, winter reminds us that God created a regular order in nature, worthy of trust. The contrast between summer and winter also teaches that each season has its place in the divine plan. On a moral level, winter becomes a biblical image of laziness or difficulty: it is a time that tests our faithfulness and diligence. Finally, the existence of winter and summer houses among the wealthy illustrates how wealth can distance us from dependence on God.

sens: son of Hur and Caleb, father of Beth-Gader
H2780.detail: Hareph is a man from the tribe of Judah living during the time of Egypt and the desert. He belongs to the lineage of Caleb and is the father of Beth-Gader, a locality in Judah (1 Chronicles 2:51). He is the brother of several other leaders of Judahite families, including Shobal, Salma, and Jezreel.
H2780.origine: The name Hareph literally means "a tearing" or "a plucking off" in Hebrew, evoking the idea of something that is separated or cut off. This name belonged to an important family of the tribe of Judah, descended from Caleb, one of the major figures in the conquest of Canaan.
H2780.emploi: Hareph is mentioned only once in the entire Bible, in 1 Chronicles 2:51, in the detailed genealogy of the descendants of Judah. He appears in the list of the sons of Hur and the descendants of Caleb, highlighting his genealogical significance within the people of Judah in its origins.

sens: Words of contempt, insult, or mockery directed at someone
Shame or dishonor that results and attaches to a person
Object of mockery or contempt for others
State of loss of dignity or reputation
H2781.detail:
1. Opprobrium is primarily a word, an insult hurled at someone to humiliate them: it is to tease, mock, or ridicule (Psalms 22:7: "All those who see me mock me"). The word evokes the sound of mockery, the tone of insults that wound.
2. This word also designates the shame and dishonor that result from these words or a shameful situation: Rachel suffers from her barrenness as a shame she bears (Genesis 30:23: "God has taken away my reproach"), meaning the state of disgrace linked to her inability to bear children.
3. Opprobrium can also refer to a person themselves, who becomes a living symbol of mockery in the eyes of others: Jeremiah says that Judah becomes "a subject of execration, horror, cursing, and reproach" (Jeremiah 42:18), meaning a target of public disdain.
4. More broadly, it is the loss of reputation and dignity that attaches to someone or a people because of their guilt or misfortunes: Ezekiel denounces Jerusalem as "an object of reproach for the nations" (Ezekiel 22:4).
H2781.origine: The Hebrew word חֶרְפָּה (cherpa) comes from a root that evokes the idea of tearing or piercing, then wounding by word. It is related to other Hebrew words expressing criticism, reproach, or offense. In Hebrew, opprobrium is what wounds the honor and dignity of a person or a people, an offense that leaves a lasting moral mark.
H2781.emploi: The word opprobrium appears 72 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, especially in the Psalms, the Prophets (Jeremiah, Ezekiel, Isaiah), and historical narratives. It designates sometimes the insult uttered (Psalms 69:20-21, where enemies overwhelm the psalmist with reproaches), sometimes the shame endured (Genesis 30:23, Rachel's barrenness), sometimes the people or the city subjected to the contempt of the nations (Ezekiel 22:4). In the Psalms, it is often the opprobrium of enemies or mockers that torments the righteous (Psalms 22:7; 44:14; 79:4). The Prophets use it to describe divine judgment: the unfaithful people become reproach in the midst of the nations (Jeremiah 42:18; Ezekiel 5:14). Opprobrium can also be erased or taken away by God, marking salvation or redemption (Isaiah 25:8; Isaiah 54:4).
H2781.portee: Opprobrium reminds us of the deep pain caused by mockery and public shame, and also how sin or misfortune can expose a people to disdain. But the Bible also shows us that God sees this humiliation, that He can erase it, and that He defends the honor of His people (Psalms 74:22). For the believer, it is an invitation not to fear the opprobrium of the world (Isaiah 51:7), for God Himself can transform shame into glory.

sens: To cut, make a clear separation between two things
To move quickly and decisively
To make a firm decision, to pronounce a judgment or will
To fix, determine something definitively
H2782.detail:
1. The word first evokes the action of cutting or slicing cleanly: this is why it means to create a clear separation, a marked distinction. When the Bible says that no dog will "move its tongue" in Egypt during the plagues (Exodus 11:7), it uses this verb to express an absolute separation between the fate of Israel and that of Egypt.
2. By extension, the verb designates a quick and decisive movement, an action executed without hesitation. When David is urged to "hurry" upon hearing a noise in the mulberry trees (2 Samuel 5:24), the word calls for swift and resolute action.
3. The most common meaning in the biblical text is to decide or pronounce a definitive judgment. The king says to his servant: "This is your judgment; you have pronounced it yourself" (1 Kings 20:40), meaning that the servant has set his own condemnation by his actions.
4. Finally, the verb expresses the idea of fixing or determining something unshakably, like a sentence or a divine decree. Job asserts that his days are "fixed" (Job 14:5), established by God without being able to be changed.
H2782.origine: The Hebrew verb חָרַץ comes from a root that suggests the action of cutting, slicing cleanly. This image of cutting or clear separation underlies all its uses: to cut is to separate, to separate is to differentiate, and to differentiate is to decide. From this root derive other words related to the notion of sharpness or decision. The initial image of sharpness or clarity naturally extends to the realm of will and judgment.
H2782.emploi: The verb appears 11 times in the Old Testament, mainly in historical narratives (Exodus, Joshua, 2 Samuel, 1 Kings) and in prophetic texts (Isaiah, Daniel). In the account of the plagues of Egypt and in Joshua, it describes a restrained action or the absence of movement in a context of divine distinction. In 2 Samuel 5:24, it calls for military action. In 1 Kings 20:40, it expresses a pronounced judgment. In wisdom literature such as Job 14:5, it speaks of the fixing of the limits of human life. In prophetic texts (Isaiah, Daniel), the verb, often in the passive voice, designates the irrevocable divine decree concerning the end times or destruction.
H2782.portee: This word invites the reader to understand that divine decisions are sharp and definitive, not hesitant or provisional. Hearing about what God has "resolved" or "fixed" reminds us that human history flows according to God's plan, predetermined and executed with certainty. This can both reassure the believer (God controls the future) and challenge them on the necessity to respond promptly to God's call.

sens: One of the two glands located in the lower back, on either side of the spine
The region of the kidneys, the lower back
The seat of emotions and inner life
H2783.detail:
1. The kidney refers to the gland itself, a paired organ located in the lower back. It is the actual, anatomical organ.
2. By extension, the word refers to the region of the kidneys, that is, the lower back, the area of the hips and pelvis. In Daniel 5:6, when King Belshazzar sees the mysterious writing on the palace wall, his terror is so profound that "the joints of his kidneys were loosened" — his entire body weakened, his legs could no longer support him.
3. In Hebrew biblical thought, the kidneys, like the heart, are the seat of deep emotions and intentions. They represent inner life, consciousness, the most secret intimacy of man.
H2783.origine: The Hebrew word חֲרַץ (cha.rats) literally refers to the anatomical organ of the kidney. In biblical Hebrew, the kidneys often appear alongside the heart to express the totality of a person's inner and emotional life. This association of the physical and the moral is characteristic of the Hebrew view of man, which does not separate body and soul.
H2783.emploi: The word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Daniel 5:6. In this context of terror before divine judgment, the image of the kidneys loosening expresses the physical and spiritual failure of the king in the face of the divine message. It is a very concrete way of showing that divine terror paralyzes man in both body and being.
H2783.portee: This verse reminds us that God's judgment is never a purely mental affair: it seizes the whole man, body and soul. The fear of the Lord manifests physically, shaking our certainties and strengths. It invites us to take seriously the reality of divine judgment and the gravity of our responsibility before Him.

sens: Physical link that holds someone captive
Suffering or affliction that oppresses
State of servitude or bondage
Moral torment or constraint
H2784.detail:
1. The word primarily refers to a material link, a chain or shackles that hold a prisoner or slave — what physically binds and prevents freedom of movement. In Isaiah 58:6, it speaks of "the chains of wickedness" that must be "loosed," an image of bonds that hinder the oppressed.
2. By extension, the word evokes suffering and torment — the pangs or torments that afflict body and soul. In Psalms 73:4, it is said of the wicked that "no torment afflicts them," suggesting that physical evil or suffering does not grip them.
3. The word can also represent servitude, the state of slavery or forced dependence on someone. This is the meaning that appears when one "breaks" the chains to free the oppressed.
4. More broadly, it denotes anything that morally oppresses — an invisible but just as real constraint as an iron chain.
H2784.origine: The Hebrew word חַרְצֻבָּה (char.tsub.bah) comes from a root that evokes the idea of binding, enclosing, or holding tightly. Its primary image is that of an object that grips, constricts, immobilizes — like a chain or tight bonds around the body. This root appears infrequently in the Old Testament, but it always carries the idea of physical or moral constraint.
H2784.emploi: The word chain appears only twice in the Hebrew Bible, in Psalms 73:4 and Isaiah 58:6. In Psalms 73:4, it qualifies the torments that do not afflict the prosperous wicked — the context suggests physical or spiritual suffering. In Isaiah 58:6, it refers to the "chains of wickedness" that must be "loosed" to free the oppressed, and the "bonds of servitude" to be broken. In this latter passage, the prophet speaks of spiritual and social liberation: the bonds that enslave the weak must be shattered. Both usages illustrate how the word shifts from personal torment to collective oppression.
H2784.portee: This word reminds us that any form of slavery — whether physical, moral, or spiritual — is a biblical reality and an evil to be fought against. For the Christian, it evokes the deliverance that God grants to those who are oppressed, as well as the call to free others from the chains of wickedness and servitude. It is a word that speaks of freedom regained in God.

sens: Hard seed or pit contained in the fruit
Insignificant product of the grape
What is despicable or worthless
H2785.detail:
1. A seed is the small hard grain found inside a fruit, such as a grape or an apple. In Numbers 6:4, the Nazarite must not eat any part of the grape, from the seeds to the skin, which shows that the seed is a distinct and consumable part of the fruit.
2. The word more broadly designates anything that comes from the vine and seems insignificant or of little value — even the seeds, even the skins, nothing should be consumed. It is the most humble product of the grape.
3. By extension, the seed symbolizes what is tiny, negligible, or unimportant: by forbidding even the seeds, the Nazarite renounces all products of the vine, from the most noble to the most humble.
H2785.origine: The Hebrew word חַרְצַנִּים (chats·zan·nim) is a plural that describes small hard objects. The term comes from Semitic roots denoting what is small, hard, or fragmented. As a product of the grape deemed insignificant, this word reflects the Hebrew perception of small or worthless things in nature.
H2785.emploi: This word appears only once in the Bible, in Numbers 6:4. It is found in the context of the law of the Nazarite, the vow of separation consecrated to God. This law enumerates the products of the vine that the Nazarite must abstain from: wine, vinegar of wine, fresh grapes, dried grapes, and specifically everything that comes from the vine, "from the seeds to the skin of the grape." The seed thus appears as the example of the most despised product, to show that the Nazarite's abstinence must be total and without exception, even for insignificant things.
H2785.portee: The choice to mention the seeds alongside the skin teaches a spiritual truth: consecration to God requires complete and uncompromising obedience, down to the smallest detail. Nothing is too small to be neglected when one commits to serve the Lord. What seems insignificant to us (a seed, a detail) matters to God and tests our faithfulness.

sens: To grind or clench one's teeth against each other
To express rage, hatred, or intense hostility
To show contempt or disdain towards someone
H2786.detail:
1. The word literally describes the sound heard when one clenches their teeth tightly, rubbing them against each other. It is an involuntary physical gesture, a contraction of the body under strong emotion (Job 16:9: God "grinds His teeth against me").
2. In Israel, grinding teeth primarily expresses the rage and hatred felt towards an enemy, like the silent explosion of fury that cannot be contained. It is the gesture of one who is boiling with anger (Psalms 37:12: "The wicked plots against the just, and grinds his teeth against him").
3. Grinding teeth can also signify contempt, disgust, or a desire to harm. It is an act of hostility that often accompanies threats or insults (Lamentations 2:16: the enemies "sneer, they grind their teeth").
H2786.origine: The Hebrew word חָרַק (haraq) expresses the dry, shrill sound of a hard object grinding. The root evokes a raw, voluntary or involuntary action of friction. It is a concrete word that describes a real sound before being applied to human emotions.
H2786.emploi: The verb appears 5 times, only in Psalms, Job, and Lamentations — books that speak of suffering, justice, and injustice. Each time, it is a gesture of hostility: God Himself grinds His teeth in anger (Job 16:9), but more often it is the wicked, the enemies, the oppressors who grind their teeth against the just or against Jerusalem (Psalms 35:16; 37:12; 112:10; Lamentations 2:16). Grinding always accompanies a malicious intent: to reach, destroy, humiliate.
H2786.portee: This word confronts us with the reality of hatred and violence, even silent ones. It reminds us that hostility towards the just is a spiritual reality against which we must remain vigilant. Grinding teeth also shows that a heart filled with wickedness cannot remain hidden — it will eventually express itself in the body and gesture. For the believer, this word emphasizes the importance of forgiveness and trust in God in the face of attacks from enemies.

sens: To be consumed by fire, to be scorched
To experience an intense sensation of heat or fever
To blaze with anger or emotion
To cause combustion, to ignite
H2787.detail:
1. To be consumed by fire, to be scorched: the word describes what happens to a material when fire ravages it. In Ezekiel 15:4-5, the wood of the vine, burned by fire, becomes unusable; it is an image of divine judgment that destroys what is not good.
2. To experience an intense sensation of heat or fever: the word can refer to the internal burning of a body consumed by illness or suffering. In Job 30:30, the bones of the sick "burn" and dry up — a poignant image of extreme physical pain.
3. To blaze with anger or emotion: fire then becomes an image of unleashed passion. In Proverbs 26:21, a quarrelsome man "kindles" a dispute like charcoal rekindles a fire — the quarrel grows and intensifies through his fiery words.
4. To cause combustion, to ignite: the verb can also mean the action of igniting something or someone. In Jeremiah 6:29, the "bellows" are burning because they are used to stoke the fire of the furnace.
H2787.origine: The root חרר expresses the idea of heat that consumes and destroys. In Hebrew, the same root gives rise to terms related to burning, ardor, and dryness. The Aramaic equivalent חרך ("to singe") shows that this notion extends throughout the Semitic West Asia. The word evokes less the flame as a poetic image than a physical reality: the drying, calcination, destruction that only fire can produce.
H2787.emploi: The verb appears about ten times in the Old Testament, mainly in the wisdom and prophetic books. In Job and Psalms, it describes the physical and spiritual suffering of the just: the bones that "burn" (Job 30:30, Psalms 102:4). In Proverbs, it figuratively depicts passion that ignites (Proverbs 26:21). In the prophets, especially Ezekiel and Jeremiah, it paints the divine judgment: the fire that consumes Jerusalem (Ezekiel 24:10-11), the furnace of punishment (Jeremiah 6:29). The word always retains this dimension of irreversible destruction: what burns does not return to its previous state.
H2787.portee: This word helps the reader grasp the intensity of divine judgment and human suffering in the Bible. When the prophets say that the land "burns" under the curse, it is not an abstract threat: it is a concrete reality of total destruction. Conversely, when the Psalms speak of the fever of the just, the verb "to burn" makes it clear that pain is a lived reality, not denied. This word thus enriches biblical prayer by giving tangible form to the emotions and judgments of God.

sens: Arid and barren area, dried by the sun
Desert region where extreme heat prevails
State of spiritual dryness and isolation
H2788.detail:
1. The word concretely designates a region or place completely dried out by heat, where no greenery grows. In Jeremiah 17:6, the cursed man "dwells in the burnt places of the desert," a land where water is lacking and where life is impossible.
2. It is a landscape of total desolation: no shade, no refuge, no food. The image evokes the most inhospitable areas of the desert, where the sun consumes everything and where even wild beasts hardly venture.
3. The Bible uses this image to depict the spiritual condition of one who turns away from God: they find themselves alone, without resources, without hope — exactly like a lost traveler in a burnt desert.
H2788.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that expresses the idea of burning and drying, related to verbs meaning "to burn" or "to be hot." The basic image is that of the sun's fire consuming the moisture and life of the earth. It is a very concrete and physical word, rooted in the experience of the Middle Eastern climate.
H2788.emploi: The word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Jeremiah 17:6. There it describes the punishment of one who turns away from the Lord and places their trust in man: instead of finding blessing and prosperity, they are condemned to dwell in a burnt and barren region, without life or comfort. It is a powerful contrast with the preceding verse (17:5) which speaks of the blessing of the just.
H2788.portee: This word reminds us that distancing oneself from God brings only desolation and spiritual death. Dwelling in a "burnt place" is the natural consequence of a lack of faith and trust in God. For the Christian, it is a call to remain rooted in the presence and word of God, the source of living water, rather than to dry up in isolation and unbelief.

sens: Vessel or container made of fired clay
Fragment or shard of pottery
Material of clay or dust
Tool or object shaped from clay
H2789.detail:
1. The primary meaning is a vessel, a container shaped from fired clay. It is ordinary, fragile pottery used in the home or for worship. In Leviticus 6:21, a clay vessel in which something has been cooked must be broken after use, as the porous clay absorbs residues; in Leviticus 14:5, a bird is slaughtered over a clay vessel filled with living water for a purification rite.
2. The word also refers to a piece, a shard, a fragment of broken pottery. Job 2:8 provides the most striking image: Job, afflicted with sores, "took a shard to scrape himself," thus using a sharp fragment to relieve his suffering.
3. By extension, earthenware evokes the clay itself, the raw and crumbly material. In Psalms 22:16, the distressed psalmist says: "My strength is dried up like clay," comparing his weakness to the drying and hardening of clay.
4. The word can also refer to an object or tool shaped from earthenware, used for a specific purpose.
H2789.origine: The Hebrew word חֶרֶשׂ (cheresh) likely comes from a root meaning "to form," "to shape." It simply describes what is shaped from earth—the raw material of the potter. The semantic field encompasses both the material (clay, earth) and the finished product (vessel, pottery). It is an ordinary word from ancient daily life, where pottery is ubiquitous.
H2789.emploi: The word appears sixteen times in the Old Testament, primarily in the purity laws of Leviticus. It regularly designates vessels or containers used for ritual or domestic purposes (Leviticus 6:21, 14:5, 15:12—in contexts of offerings or purification). Leviticus emphasizes that earthenware, once ritually contaminated, must be broken and not simply washed, as it is porous. Outside of the law, the word appears in poetic comparisons: Job uses it as a scraper in his suffering (Job 2:8), and the psalmist compares his waning energy to clay that dries up (Psalms 22:16). Isaiah 30:14 uses the image of a clay vessel that breaks: divine power shatters human pride mercilessly, just as pottery is broken without care. The word thus operates both in a literal sense (container, debris) and in a figurative sense (fragility, dust).
H2789.portee: Earthenware speaks of human fragility and dependence on God. A clay vessel is something simple, inexpensive, easily breakable—an image of mortal condition. The laws regarding pottery also remind us that impurity clings to us as it clings to porous clay: a superficial washing is not enough; a clear break with evil is necessary. For the believer, this word invites us not to take pride in our fragility but to seek our strength in God alone.

sens: To work the land with a plow to prepare it for sowing
To engrave, trace, or cut a shape into a hard material
To imagine, conceive, or combine plans in one's heart
To invent or create objects through artisan work
H2790A.detail:
1. To plow the land is the primary meaning of the word: it is the work of the farmer who breaks the soil with his plow to make it fertile and ready to receive seeds. Isaiah 28:24 shows this: "Does the one who plows for sowing plow continually?"—plowing is the natural preparation before the harvest.
2. To engrave or trace means to imprint a lasting mark in a material: Jeremiah 17:1 speaks of sin "engraved on the tablet of their heart," as if letters were being carved into it. This is a work of precision and depth.
3. To meditate on plans or thoughts borrows the image of plowing for reflection: one "cultivates" ideas in their heart, whether good or bad. Proverbs 6:18 describes the heart that "meditates on wicked plans"—one manufactures evil as one works the land.
4. To invent or create instruments extends this idea: it is to shape something new. Genesis 4:22 mentions Tubal-Cain who "forged all kinds of tools of bronze and iron"—he worked metal as a plowman works the land.
H2790A.origine: The Hebrew verb חָרַשׁ (charash) comes from a root that evokes the action of digging, breaking, tracing a deep line. It is a concrete word first—plowing—that has extended to all works requiring digging, shaping, combining: engraving, forging, and even the thought that "digs" in the heart. The noun "plowman" (charash) and "plow" come from the same family.
H2790A.emploi: The word appears 24 times in the Hebrew Bible, mainly in wisdom poetry (Proverbs, Job, Psalms) and in the prophets. In its literal sense, it describes the plowing of the land (Isaiah 28:24, Hosea 10:11) and the work of the artisan (Genesis 4:22). In its figurative sense, very frequent, it designates the mental elaboration of plans—especially wicked ones: one "plows iniquity" (Job 4:8), one "meditates on evil" (Proverbs 6:18, 12:20, 14:22). This extension of the word from physical work to thought is typically biblical: it shows that conceiving evil is to cultivate it, to sow it.
H2790A.portee: This word reminds the believer that our thoughts and plans are like land that we plow: we sow in it, and we will reap the fruits (Galatians 6:7-8 echoes Job 4:8). Meditating on evil is already to cultivate it within us. Conversely, cultivating wisdom and justice is to prepare a harvest of life. The word invites vigilance: what are we sowing in our hearts?

sens: To keep silent, not to speak
To remain silent in the face of something, without intervening
Not to hear, to be deaf to
To silence someone, to bring them to silence
To remain inactive, not to act
H2790B.detail:
1. To be silent simply means to keep quiet, to refrain from speaking. It is the attitude of one who says nothing: Abraham "without saying anything" observes Rebekah (Genesis 24:21), or Job invites his friends to "keep silent" and listen to him (Job 13:13).
2. Silence can be a form of tacit consent: a father who "keeps silent" regarding his daughter's vow implicitly approves it (Numbers 30:15).
3. Sometimes the word expresses indifference or refusal to act: God Himself "does not speak," remains inactive in the face of injustice (Psalms 50:21, Habakkuk 1:13), which heightens the anxious expectation of the one who begs Him not to remain silent (Psalms 109:1).
4. Silence can also signify powerlessness or an inability to respond: Job asks his friends to let him speak rather than to "silence" people with empty words (Job 11:3).
5. In a context of caution, to be silent means to keep a secret: Jeremiah "says nothing" to his enemies about the king's plan (Jeremiah 38:27).
H2790B.origine: The Hebrew verb חָרֵשׁ (charesh) comes from a root that fundamentally means "to be mute," "to be deprived of speech." This root is close to the idea of deafness or mutism. It is related to other Hebrew words denoting silence or inactivity. The word can also evoke the work of a farmer who works "in silence," hence the secondary meaning of "to refrain from acting" or "to remain inactive."
H2790B.emploi: This verb appears 43 times in the Old Testament, especially in the Psalms, Job, and historical narratives. It primarily expresses the action of keeping silent in daily life: Abraham observes without speaking, a father approves by remaining silent. It also denotes silence in the face of injustice or a call: the Psalms implore God not to remain mute before the suffering of the righteous. Job uses it to invite silence and listening: it is sometimes wise to "silence people" instead of responding with vain words (Job 11:3, Proverbs 17:28). In political or secret contexts, to be silent means to exercise caution: Jeremiah reveals nothing to his adversaries. The verb also carries a strong theological meaning: God who "does not speak" or "is silent" remains master of the world, but this inaction can also be a judgment or a trial.
H2790B.portee: For the Christian, this word invites a distinction between two silences: that of wisdom, which listens and refrains from vain words, and that of cowardice, which abandons the righteous to their fate. It also teaches that God's silence is never forgetfulness, but expectation or judgment. Keeping silent can be an act of faith, as seen in Abraham who trusts the Lord without contesting, or an act of obedience, as in submission to the decisions of others. Conversely, an authentic biblical complaint implores God not to remain mute.

sens: In a hidden manner, without noise or publicity
In silence, without witnesses
Without anyone knowing or seeing
H2791A.detail:
1. The word describes an action carried out discreetly, away from prying eyes and without making noise. Joshua sends two spies "secretly" from Shittim: this departure must remain unknown so that the inhabitants of Jericho do not discover what is being prepared (Joshua 2:1).

2. The adverb evokes the idea of silence and caution: one acts without attracting attention, without shouting, without anyone noticing. It is discretion in action, the opposite of a public or displayed approach.

3. Implicitly, the word carries the idea of a kept secret, of confidentiality: what happens in private must remain among the initiated, far from enemy ears.
H2791A.origine: The Hebrew root evokes silence and deafness. It is also used to describe one who is mute or deprived of hearing. The adverb "secretly" naturally derives from this: to act in silence means to act without anyone hearing it, thus in secret.
H2791A.emploi: This word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Joshua 2:1. There, Joshua sends two spies "secretly" before entering the Promised Land: the context is military and strategic. The secret is a tactical necessity — the mission must remain unknown to the enemies to succeed. The word emphasizes the importance of discretion for God's plan to be fulfilled without hindrance.
H2791A.portee: This account teaches that God uses natural means — here, caution and strategy — to guide His people. The secret is not contrary to trust in God; it is often an act of wisdom. For the Christian, this reminds us of the importance of caution and discretion when the situation demands it, and that God can accomplish His work through discreet means, away from the spotlight.

sens: Secret knowledge in hidden or mysterious domains
Magic, enchantment, occult practices
Fearsome skill, power that inspires awe
H2791B.detail:
1. The word designates hidden knowledge, an art that cannot be easily understood or imitated — like magic or enchantment. In Isaiah 3:3, "the skillful enchanter" translates this term: it refers to someone who possesses mysterious and fearsome knowledge.
2. More broadly, it refers to magic itself, this set of occult practices that the Bible often warns against. The word suggests powers that are extraordinary and cannot be explained by natural means.
3. The term also carries the idea of a skill that inspires fear or respect, almost fear: it is a formidable power, that of someone who knows things that others do not.
H2791B.origine: The Hebrew root refers to what is "hidden" or "secret." The Hebrew word cheresh (חרש) primarily evokes silence and mystery — what is concealed, veiled, incomprehensible. From this comes the meaning of "hidden art" or "occult practice": it is knowledge that is not disclosed, reserved for those who possess it.
H2791B.emploi: The word appears only once in the Bible in Isaiah 3:3. It is used to describe one of the important figures that God will remove from Judah as punishment: "the skillful enchanter." In this context, Isaiah lists all the supports of society — the leaders, warriors, judges, prophets, artisans — and shows that God will take them away. The enchanter is among these powerful and respected figures, indicating that at the time of Isaiah, practitioners of magic enjoyed a certain authority or influence. The word suggests a form of human power — occult and seductive — that God is about to destroy.
H2791B.portee: This word reminds us that the Bible rejects magic and occult practices, not as mere superstitions, but as rival forms of power that claim to know the future or control hidden forces. For the Christian, this underscores the importance of trusting God alone and rejecting the temptation to seek elsewhere — in divination, spells, or occult powers — what only God can provide. Isaiah shows that these human powers, however prestigious they may seem, are fragile in the face of God's judgment.

sens: A Levite during the time of exile and return
H2792.detail: Heresch is a Levite mentioned only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 9:15, alongside Bakbakkar, Galal, and Matthania. He belonged to the service of the tabernacle during the period of exile and return to Jerusalem.
H2792.origine: The name Heresch literally means "mute" in Hebrew, formed from the root that denotes silence or the absence of speech. Although the meaning of the name is clear, it is unknown why this Levite received this particular name — perhaps due to a disability, or perhaps a nickname whose context is lost to us.
H2792.emploi: Heresch appears only once in the Scriptures, in 1 Chronicles 9:15, in a list of Levites who performed various functions at the tabernacle. He is named among the temple servants at the time of the restoration of worship after the exile, showing that Levites of all origins and names participated in the renewal of Israel's religious life.

sens: A wooded place in Judea
H2793G.detail: Horech is a wooded area located in Judea, where David hides during his flight from Saul. The name comes from the Hebrew חֹרֶשׁ (horesh), which literally means "forest" or "wood": it is a place of refuge amidst the trees.
H2793G.origine: The name Horech is derived from the Hebrew root חרש (harash), which evokes the idea of a forest, a wooded and wild place. Such locations provided natural protection for fugitives in ancient times.
H2793G.emploi: Horech appears four times in the First Book of Samuel (chapters 23), all in the account of David's flight from Saul. It is in this forest that David and Jonathan meet to bid farewell and swear friendship before David must escape elsewhere. Horech is thus the setting for one of the most moving encounters between the two friends: it is there that Jonathan comes to encourage David and reassure him about God's will (1 Samuel 23:16).
H2793G.portee: This place symbolizes the refuge that God offers to those who seek Him, even in distress and persecution. David, unjustly pursued, finds both physical safety and spiritual comfort in this wood; it is a reminder that God provides for our needs in times of trial.

sens: A mass of trees covering an area, forest
Mountainous terrain covered with trees
Dense foliage of a tree
H2793H.detail: 1. The most direct meaning is that of a forest or a wooded expanse: an area covered with trees. When King Jotham "built castles and towers in the woods" (2 Chronicles 27:4), he constructs in forested mountainous areas, far from cities. 2. By extension, the word also refers to the wooded height itself, the crown or summit covered with trees. Isaiah speaks of the "tops of the mountains" where strong cities will be abandoned "before the children of Israel" (Isaiah 17:9), as if swept away by a superior force. 3. When referring to a particular tree, the word can also mean the thick foliage that crowns it. Ezekiel describes Assyria in the figure of a cedar whose "foliage was thick" (Ezekiel 31:3), an image of its power and magnificence.
H2793H.origine: The Hebrew word חֹרֶשׁ (horesh) comes from a root that expresses the idea of a covered area, densely planted. Its fundamental meaning is that of a natural wooded space, as opposed to cultivated or inhabited land. The same root can refer to the forest itself, the wooded area, or the aspect of what is covered with dense vegetation.
H2793H.emploi: The word appears only three times in the Hebrew Bible, always to describe natural spaces or images of vegetative power. In 2 Chronicles, it refers to a geographical reality: wooded mountainous areas where the king builds fortifications. In the prophets (Isaiah and Ezekiel), wood becomes an image: an image of desolation in Isaiah, an image of majestic grandeur in Ezekiel with the cedar of Lebanon. The word appears rarely, which emphasizes its use in important contexts.
H2793H.portee: Wood or forest reminds the Christian reader that God masters nature and history. The castles in the woods show how God protects His people through concrete means. The prophetic images of vegetative power or desolation invite reflection on the greatness of God and the fragility of human empires, as imposing as a great cedar.

sens: unable to hear
willfully refusing to listen
not hearing the word of God
H2795.detail:
1. In the literal sense, the word refers to one who cannot hear, who is deprived of hearing. This is a physical disability that the Bible recognizes and for which it commands respect for those affected: Leviticus 19:14 prohibits cursing a deaf person, showing that this individual has rights to be respected.

2. The word is also used figuratively for one who willfully refuses to listen. Psalm 38:14 illustrates this: "I am like a deaf man, I do not hear," meaning that the psalmist does not respond to those who provoke him — it is a choice. Similarly, in Psalm 58:5, the serpent is called "deaf" because it deliberately shuts its ear to the words of the charmer.

3. Deafness also becomes an image of spiritual unbelief. In Isaiah 42:18-19 and 43:8, Israel is called deaf to symbolize its refusal to hear the word of God. But Isaiah 35:5 announces a messianic reversal: "The ears of the deaf will be opened," a promise that Jesus will fulfill by healing the infirm.
H2795.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that describes the absence or inability to hear. It is found in terms that speak of mutism or impermeability to sound. The basic image is that of an ear "closed" or not functioning. In the biblical context, the word can also take on a moral dimension: one who does not want to hear is "deaf" in the sense of being willfully closed off.
H2795.emploi: The word appears 9 times in biblical Hebrew, primarily in the prophetic books. In Exodus 4:11, God presents Himself as the one who makes men deaf or seeing — physical disability comes from the Creator and is not a shame. The laws of Israel protect the deaf: Leviticus 19:14 prohibits their exploitation. The psalms use it as an image of voluntary silence (Psalm 38:14) or refusal to obey (Psalm 58:5). But above all, Isaiah makes it a central symbol: Israel is deaf to the word of the Lord (Isaiah 42:18-19; 43:8), and only the Messiah will heal this spiritual deafness (Isaiah 29:18; 35:5). The healing of the deaf thus becomes a hallmark of the advent of salvation.
H2795.portee: This word teaches us that physical deafness is not a moral defect: God sometimes creates it, and the deaf deserve respect and protection. But it also invites us to examine ourselves spiritually: are we "deaf" to the voice of God? Do we refuse to listen to His word? The messianic promise of Isaiah shows that Jesus comes to heal not only the body but especially the heart closed to God.

sens: Skilled worker in a manual trade: carpenter, blacksmith, engraver, sculptor
One who manufactures or shapes something with skill and intention
Figuratively: one who prepares, organizes, sets in place (referring to an action or destruction)
H2796.detail:
1. The word primarily designates a skilled worker in the trades of wood, metal, or stone. In Exodus 28:11, the engraver must carve the names of the sons of Israel on the stones of the ephod with precision, as one engraves a seal. In 2 Samuel 5:11, the carpenters of Tyre build David's house, a task that requires expertise. It refers to a tradesman, trained, who knows how to do his work.
2. The word expands to include anyone who manufactures or creates a work: a blacksmith who shapes iron, a sculptor who works wood or stone to make an idol. Isaiah 41:7 shows the "sculptor" encouraging the founder, both artisans working together to create an image.
3. By extension, the word takes on a figurative meaning and applies to the creator or organizer of a work, even an abstract one. In Isaiah 54:16, God says: "I have created the worker who blows the coals in the fire" and also "the destroyer" — indicating that those who make or unmake things are artisans in service of the divine plan.
H2796.origine: The Hebrew root חרש (cha-rash) refers to the idea of making, manufacturing, working with one's hands and intelligence. It evokes the action of shaping, creating a form from a material. The word initially applies to the trades of wood, metal, and stone, where the artisan's work transforms raw material into a useful or beautiful object.
H2796.emploi: The word appears 34 times in the Old Testament, mainly in construction narratives (of the Tabernacle, the Temple, royal houses) and in the prophets. In building contexts, it designates skilled workers paid for their labor (2 Kings 12:11; 2 Chronicles 34:11). In the prophets, Isaiah and Jeremiah use it to criticize artisans who make idols (Isaiah 40:19-20; Jeremiah 10:3-9): the word then emphasizes that the idol is a human creation, a product of labor, not a deity. The context varies from simple factual narrative (a craftsman builds) to ironic critique (a craftsman makes his own god).
H2796.portee: This word opens the believer's eyes to the dignity of manual labor and expertise. Every artisan who practices his trade honestly participates in the order created by God.
